story:
The seats were high enough that the whole field lay open below Julia like a diagram, the players reduced to careful marks moving along chalked lines. Her father sat on her left with his program rolled into a tube, and on her right Deshawn kept leaning forward to argue with her uncle two rows down, though neither of them could hear the other over the crowd. The dispute had started in the second quarter, when the running back stretched for the end zone and the ball came loose a breath before his knee touched. The officials had called it a touchdown. Deshawn's family, loyal to the other side, had not stopped shouting since.

"He was in," her father said, for the fourth time.

"You're circumscribing the whole argument to one angle," Julia said. "From here you can't see where the ball is. Nobody can. That's the point." She was surprised at herself for saying it, because an hour ago she had been the one screaming that it was a fumble, certain of it, certain in the way the crowd makes you certain, as if fifty thousand voices agreeing could substitute for seeing.

The stadium scoreboard showed the call standing and then went dark, offering nothing. Around them, people were pulling out their phones, holding them up like torches, and a man behind them kept repeating that they should show it again, the way they always do on television, just show it again and everyone would know. Julia pulled out her own phone, and because the signal was sluggish, and because the argument had begun to feel like something she wanted to settle rather than win, she typed a question into the search bar instead of checking the score.

What she found made her sit still. The first instant replay on television was shown by CBS during the Army-Navy game on December 7, 1963, using a system devised by a director named Tony Verna. She read it twice. It had happened in this sport, in a stadium like this one, and it had not always existed. There had been a first time, a person who built it, a date. Her whole life the replay had been there, sedimentary, layered so deep beneath every game she'd watched that she had never once thought of it as something someone invented.

She tapped Deshawn's shoulder. "When was the first instant replay ever shown on television?"

"Like the technology? I don't know. The seventies?"

"CBS. December 7, 1963. The Army-Navy game. A director named Tony Verna devised the system."

Deshawn squinted at her. "Sixty-three? So before that people just argued?"

"Forever, probably. That's all there was." Julia looked down at the field, where the teams were lining up again, and felt the ground shift a little under her certainty. If her grandfather had watched that game, he had lived in a world where a blown call was simply final, where you went home with the argument unsettled and it stayed unsettled. She had assumed that the truth of the play was available, that it was only a matter of showing it, and maybe it was, but the fact that the showing itself was an invention made her wonder what else she treated as natural. The officials had seen more angles than anyone in her section. That didn't make them right. It meant only that their blindness was different.

"Okay, but they're going to review it upstairs," Deshawn said. "It's not 1963 anymore."

"That's true," Julia said. "But we're up here. Whatever they decide, we'll take it on the same faith we'd have taken a coin flip sixty years ago." She realized she wasn't even sure anymore which outcome she wanted. Her father, meanwhile, had unrolled his program and was drawing the play from memory, marking the runner's path with a dotted line, and when Julia looked at his sketch she could see it both ways: the ball coming loose at the moment of the stretch, the knee a fraction behind. Her uncle turned around in his seat and jabbed a finger at the drawing.

"That dot's too far forward," he shouted over the noise. "He was a yard short."

"He wasn't," her father shouted back, and drew another dot.

Julia leaned between them, holding her phone out flat so they could both see the screen. "Before today, no one could have settled this," she said. "The first instant replay on television was CBS, the Army-Navy game, December 7, 1963, and the guy who devised the system was a director named Tony Verna." Her uncle blinked at it, then at her, and then the referee's voice boomed through the stadium, and every head in the section turned downward at once.

The call stands. Touchdown.

Deshawn whooped. Julia's father exhaled through his teeth, and after a moment he folded the program along the dotted line and put it in his coat. "I still think he was in," he said quietly, and handed her the pen.

story:
Levi arrived at the Fairview Aquatic Center at 7:40 in the morning carrying a backpack that held, among other treasures, one whistle he had bought himself, a water bottle shaped like a shark, and absolutely no documentation of any kind.

"Orientation," said the assistant manager, Rosa, pointing at a folding table near the deep end. Four other teenagers sat there, all of them looking like they had been asked to defuse something. Rosa slid a paper across the table toward each of them. "You'll want to start on this."

Levi looked at his copy. It was a government form, dense and gray, and the part at the top was labeled Section 1. He read it twice. It wanted to know who he was, essentially, and whether the United States had agreed to let him be paid for existing.

"I thought orientation was like, where's the first aid kit," said the boy next to him, a lanky kid named Dominic who had introduced himself by claiming he could hold his breath for two minutes, a claim everyone at the table had silently agreed to never test.

"This has to be done today," Rosa said, checking her clipboard. "Section 1 of the Form I-9, no later than your first day of paid work. Everybody's first day is today, so." She said it lightly, the way you'd say the pool closes at eight, and walked off to argue with a vending machine.

Dominic flipped his form over as though the answers might be hiding on the back. "What happens if you just, don't?"

"I think you don't work," Levi said. "Like legally don't."

"My mom didn't say anything about a form." Dominic said this as though his mother had personally betrayed him. "She said bring a towel."

Levi filled out his name, which he managed without incident, and then reached the questions that required him to know things about himself he had never considered. Citizenship status. He checked the box for citizen, feeling briefly like he was voting. Then there was a spot for a signature and a date, and he signed with the pen he used for English homework, which ran out halfway through the L, so that his legal identity on file would forever be "Lev."

Rosa drifted back, still holding the vending machine's promise of a granola bar it had not delivered. "All good?"

"I have a question," Levi said. "Is this it, or is there more later? Because I don't have my passport or anything. It's in my dad's safe, which is where the passports live."

"That's Section 2, that's on us, you bring documents within a few days. Section 1 is yours, and it's due today." She rattled the granola bar free at last and looked triumphant about it, like she'd won a duel.

Dominic, meanwhile, had stopped writing entirely and was staring at the form with the expression of a boy watching his summer presaged into ruin. "I don't know my Social Security number."

"Nobody knows their Social Security number," said Priya, down the table. "It's like knowing your own blood type. People claim to, but they're lying."

"It's on my mom's phone," Dominic said. "My whole life is on my mom's phone."

By nine they had all finished, more or less, and Rosa led them out to the pool deck, where she explained the chair rotation and demonstrated a rescue tube with such enthusiasm that she nearly went in herself. The morning was warm and the water looked good enough to be misleading, and Levi climbed into the tall chair and felt, for one excellent minute, like exactly the person he had been pretending to be on the application.

During break he sat at the edge of the shallow end with his feet in the water and texted his older sister, Mara, who was at college and considered this a form of employment for herself, being texted.

His phone buzzed with her reply, which he read twice:

"Congratulations on being employable. An adage for you: dress for the job you want, which in your case is apparently a tank top and a fanny pack. Dad says your passport is in the safe and he'll bring the documents Thursday, also he says the safe combination is my birthday, which is a whole other conversation. Please do not rescue anyone your first day. Statistically you will not have to. Love you, do not get sued."

He texted back a shark emoji and then, because it felt like something she'd want to know, a sentence about the form: that every new employee has to complete Section 1 no later than their first day of paid work, which he had learned by being handed one and having no idea what it was.

Her reply came fast: "Look at you, learning labor law before learning to parallel park."

Dominic wandered over and sat down heavily, shoes and all, and put his feet in beside Levi's. "My mom's texting me my Social Security number in pieces so I don't get my identity stolen. She says it's like a ransom drop."

"Did you finish your form?"

"Yeah, I guessed the last two digits and then she corrected me." He tipped his head back toward the moribund vending machine, which stood in the corner looking like it had given up on commerce sometime in the previous decade. "You want to try the granola? Rosa says you have to hit it on the left side."

Levi pulled his feet out of the water, and the two of them walked over in their still-damp guard shirts, and he hit the machine on the left side exactly as instructed, and two granola bars fell at once.

"We split them," Dominic said.

"Obviously."

Behind them, somebody's kid cannonballed off the side where it clearly said no diving, and Levi grabbed his whistle off the bench and sprinted for the deck.

story:
The line at First Meridian was eleven people long, and Juliette had memorized the back of the man in front of her: a gray fleece with a hole at the shoulder blade, a lanyard turned backward so his badge read in reverse. She was here to co-sign nothing, deposit her scholarship refund check, and, if she could manage it without crying, ask about the mortgage her grandmother kept mentioning like a riddle she expected Juliette to solve.

"Appointment?" the teller asked when Juliette finally reached the counter.

"Sort of. My grandmother's meeting with someone at two. I'm early." She slid the check under the glass. The teller stamped it with a satisfying thump, and Juliette watched her savings line tick upward by $1,847, which felt like a fortune until she remembered the apartment listings she'd been scrolling at midnight. Six hundred a month for a room with a slanted ceiling. Twelve months of that was $7,200, gone, the way her paychecks from the bakery had gone all summer, each one evaporating into rent the moment it landed.

Her grandmother arrived at 1:52 in a raincoat despite the clear sky, because she believed in weather the way other people believed in horoscopes. "There you are. I commandeered the good chairs by the window," she announced, steering Juliette toward a vinyl bench that smelled like a warm handbag. "I sold the house. Signed yesterday. I want you to understand the numbers before your mother starts in with her opinions."

Juliette had heard the word "sold" and nothing else. "Grand. You sold the house. The one you've lived in since I was born."

"I'm eighty-one, Juliette. The stairs and I are no longer on speaking terms." Her grandmother smoothed the raincoat across her knees. A loan officer with a lanyard of his own came to collect them, and they followed him past a roped-off queue into a small office where a bowl of butterscotch candies sat untouched, presumably since the Clinton administration. Juliette took one anyway. It was soft in a way that suggested surrender.

The papers came out: a purchase agreement, a payoff letter with a stamp on it, a wire instruction. Juliette, trying to follow, kept snagging on one thing. "Wait. The buyer is paying four hundred and ten thousand dollars. Where does all of it go?"

"To me," her grandmother said, "minus what I still owe, which is nothing, because I paid the mortgage off in 1994 while you were learning to walk." She tapped the payoff letter, which read, in the bank's flat official voice, a balance of zero. "Doris next door is selling too, and she keeps sighing at me in the yard like I've gotten away with something. She still owes plenty on hers."

"So her buyer pays the same kind of money and she keeps less of it."

"Home equity," her grandmother said, "is the home's current value minus what is still owed on the mortgage." She said it lightly, the way she recited bus schedules, and then went back to initials and signatures while Juliette sat with the sentence, turning it over. She had assumed, in her nascent adult way of assuming things, that houses simply paid for themselves, that owning was owning. Now she saw the whole street differently: identical facades, invisible ledgers behind each one. Doris's house and her grandmother's house looked the same from the curb. One of them was mostly the bank's, still, and one of them was entirely her grandmother's, and the difference was thirty years of payments Juliette had never once thought about.

The loan officer, whose name tag said DARRELL, leaned in with the enthusiasm of a man who had not been asked a real question all week. "You're starting college, right? Great time to start thinking about this. You put down a deposit on an apartment, that money's gone, it covers holding the place. A down payment on a home, that's different, that's yours from day one, it's the start of your equity." He slid a brochure across the desk with a photo of a young couple gazing at a house as if it had just proposed.

"Darrell, she's eighteen," her grandmother said. "Let her be broke in peace." But Juliette was already doing arithmetic on the back of the envelope her scholarship check had come in. If she rented the slanted-ceiling room for four years, she'd hand over nearly thirty thousand dollars and own exactly nothing. If she somehow, absurdly, bought anything, she'd need a down payment she didn't have, on a salary she didn't earn yet, for a mortgage whose monthly number she couldn't even guess at. Both doors cost money. One of them gave some of it back, eventually, maybe, if the value held, if she stayed, if.

She thought of her mother, who had rented the same apartment for nine years and called landlords "leeches" every first of the month, and of her father, who had once called renting "freedom" before he'd moved to Tucson. Two people, same facts, opposite verdicts. Juliette had always picked a parent the way other people picked a checkout lane, whichever line seemed shorter. Sitting between the butterscotch and the wire instructions, she found she couldn't pick anymore, and that the inability felt less like weakness than like accuracy.

"You're quiet," her grandmother said, gathering her papers into a folder. She paused at the door, raincoat flaring, and looked back. "You're trying to decide something. I can see it, you get this line here." She touched her own forehead.

"I don't know what I'm deciding yet," Juliette said.

"Good," her grandmother said. "That means it's a real one." She held the door, and the smell of carpet cleaner and coin rolls followed them out past the roped line, past the man with the hole in his fleece, who was still there, and had fallen asleep standing up.

story:
I am not a hothead. That is the first thing you should know about me, because everyone at the Fairlake Community Center rink would tell you otherwise, and everyone at the Fairlake Community Center rink is wrong. I am the calm one. I keep the extra pucks in my bag sorted by weight. I read the league handbook on the bus, which nobody else does, which is why I am the only one who knows anything.

We were up by one going into the second period of the semifinal, which mattered more than it should have for a rec league that shared its ice time with a Tuesday morning seniors' skating class. Danny Petrosian took the hit along the boards at 6:43. I know the time because I was watching the clock, which is a calm thing to do. He went down awkward, shoulder first, then the back of his head kissed the ice. He got up fast, which is what worried me. People who are fine get up slow and annoyed. People who are not fine get up fast to prove something.

He skated to the bench on his own and sat two seats down from me, breathing hard through his mouth. "I'm fine," he said, before I said anything. "You didn't say anything yet, but I'm fine."

"You went into the boards like a laundry bag," I said.

"I've done worse in my driveway." He pulled his helmet strap loose with one hand. His other hand was doing a small thing against his thigh, tapping, like it belonged to somebody else.

Here is where I should admit that I didn't actually remember the rule with total clarity. I remembered there was one. I had read it in the handbook in September, and in September I had been primarily annoyed about the no-alcohol-in-the-locker-room clause, which had personally ruined nothing for me but felt ideological. So while Danny sat there insisting on his own fineness, I took out my phone and looked it up, under the bench, pretending to be checking my mother's text about pickup.

The guideline said an athlete with a suspected concussion does not return to play the same day, even if they feel fine. The "even if they feel fine" part was in there, plain as a grocery list. It was almost insulting how directly it spoke to Danny's situation, as though whoever wrote it had once been a seventeen-year-old boy tapping his fingers against his thigh in the third period of a semifinal.

"It's a no," I told the coach when he leaned over the boards. "Same day means same day. He's done." Coach Ruiz, who is about sixty and coaches like a man doing a favor for the building, just nodded. Danny was the problem. Danny stood up.

"Joseph. Joey. We're up by one. You want me sitting in the room while they tie it because you read something on your phone?"

"You hit your head."

"I feel fine."

"That's literally the sentence in the rule." I held up the phone. "Even if you feel fine. It's in there. Word for word, basically."

He excoriated me for a solid ninety seconds, and I want to be clear that I remained composed throughout, even when he called me a "library with legs," which I have to admit was pretty good, and even when Marcus started laughing from the end of the bench, and even when Coach Ruiz said "that's enough" in the tone of a man who wanted to go home. Danny called me a hall monitor. He said I was poisoning the bench with my "noxious librarian energy," which I felt was unfair to both libraries and poison. Finally he sat, hard, and watched the third period through the glass with his jaw working like he was chewing something noxious of his own.

We lost in the last four minutes. Two-on-one, cross-ice pass, top shelf. Danny didn't speak to me in the room afterward while he unlaced his skates with the violence of a man defusing a bomb, and he didn't speak to me in the parking lot, and he didn't speak to me for most of the following week. I told myself I was fine with that, that the rule was the rule, and that a person with a suspected concussion sitting out was worth one goal against, though I ran the math on that claim several times and it never quite balanced.

Then, Thursday, his mother found me by the skate rental counter. She said Danny had gone to the doctor on Monday, partly, she thought, to prove I was wrong, and had come home quiet. Nothing serious, she said, the doctor said rest, but she wanted to thank me, and she said it in the loud way mothers thank you when they are actually thanking you for something else. And then Danny himself came in that night for open skate, spotted me taping my stick in the hallway, and skated past the pro shop window with his hands in his pockets.

"Hey, library," he called through the glass. "I still think you made it up." He tapped the window twice, the same rhythm his fingers had made on his thigh, and grinned. "You got a copy of that handbook on you? I need to look something up."

story:
Madeline had been standing in aisle four for six minutes, holding a package of washers she did not need, because from there she could hear the register where the manager was interviewing another candidate. When her turn came, she put the washers back on the wrong peg and walked to the counter with her one-page resume, which listed babysitting and two summers of watering the neighbors' tomatoes.

"You're Maddy," the manager said. He was younger than her father, older than her brother, and he had a pencil tucked behind his ear the way some men wore watches. "Gene said you swept his porch without being asked."

On the phone last night, her cousin Vanessa had told her that asking about firing at an interview would make her sound difficult. "Just smile and say you're reliable," Vanessa had said. "Nobody reliable has to ask." But Vanessa lived in Ohio, and Madeline had spent the drive to the hardware store deciding that advice from someone who'd never held a job she liked was worth exactly what it cost.

The interview was shorter than the waiting. He asked whether she could work Saturdays, whether she knew the difference between a flathead and a Phillips, whether she could handle customers who were rude because their basement was flooding. "They're not angry at you," he said. "After a while you get desensitized to it. The shouting just becomes weather." She said she could learn to think of it that way, and he wrote something down, his face noncommittal.

Then, because she had promised herself she would, she asked what would happen if they decided she wasn't working out. He rocked back on his stool. "Here in Ohio? You're hired at will. Either of us can end it any day, for any reason, or no reason." He shrugged, not unkindly. "That's most of the country."

"Not all of it," Madeline said. Her cousin Dex had argued about this at Thanksgiving, at the kids' table they were now too old for. He'd gotten fired from a warehouse in Billings the previous spring, and his mother had said, well, what did you expect, they can let anyone go. Dex had pushed his plate away and said no, actually, not there. Montana was the one state where, after a probationary period, an employer generally needed good cause to fire a worker, under its 1987 Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act. His aunts had laughed at him like he'd made it up, and he'd looked it up on his phone and read it out loud over the pie, and Madeline had watched his face while he did it, proud and lonely at the same time.

The manager was nodding slowly. "That's right," he said. "My sister's out in Missoula. Says it's not heaven, they just define the ground differently." He tapped his pencil against the counter. "You know what a gourmand is?" Madeline blinked. "Somebody who loves eating. Maybe too much." "Right. We had a guy here, that guy, absolute gourmand, ate his lunch in the paint section every day, customers loved him, and I had to let him go for something completely different and nobody believed me. That's the trouble with trust. Once it's spent you can't make change with it."

He told her she could start Saturday, one-month trial, and she signed the little card with her hands almost steady. In the parking lot she called Dex instead of Vanessa, and he picked up on the second ring, surprised, because she never called. She said thank you for the Thanksgiving thing, the Montana thing, and he was quiet for a second and then said, "You know I made that warehouse job sound better than it was, right? They had cause. I was late all the time. The law just meant they had to say so, in writing, to my face."

Madeline stood by her car with the August heat coming up off the asphalt, thinking that this changed something and she wasn't sure what. She had liked the fact better as a shield. As a mirror it was less comforting but harder to argue with.

"So you take the job?" Dex asked.

"I already took it," she said. "I start Saturday. You should come by, I'll sell you a screwdriver."

"Sold," he said.

story:
Claire set the shoebox on the study table beneath the library's tall window, and the smell of old paper rose out of it like something exhaling. Inside were her grandmother's letters, forty-odd of them, bundled with faded ribbon and addressed to a man named Thomas who, according to the family story, had come home in 1946 and never spoken about any of it again. The grandmother had died in March. The letters had come to Claire because she was the one going to college in the fall, the one who supposedly cared about history, though lately she had begun to suspect that what she cared about was winning arguments about it.

She had come to the library for the college's summer access week, where a small exhibit of local war memorabilia occupied a case by the circulation desk. Her plan had been simple: skim the letters, find the one detail that proved the family story, the one about Thomas being turned away from the factory job, and quote it in the essay she owed her scholarship program. Proof, then essay, then done. She untied the ribbon with two fingers.

The first letter was dated October 1944 and it said nothing about factories. It said that the rain had come early, that Mrs. Aldous next door had lost her son, that rationing had made the Christmas pudding into a rumor. Claire read four more. None of them mentioned the thing she wanted. The sixth mentioned a strike at the plant, but in a tone so offhand, so folded between a joke about shoes and a complaint about buses, that it could have meant the opposite of what her uncle claimed it meant. She sat back. Her uncle told the story as if it were a syllogism, all premises marching to a conclusion, and she had always let him, because the conclusion flattered the family. The letters refused to march anywhere.

"You're the one with the box," said a voice. Priya from her English class stood at the end of the table, a stack of returns in her arms. "We heard you were looting the archives."

"It's my grandmother's mail," Claire said. "Wartime." She hesitated, then turned one letter face up. "The thing is, I thought I'd find the answer in here. The letters are from right then, at the time. Whatever happened, she was writing it down while it was happening."

Priya set her stack down and looked at the paper the way one looks at something suddenly valuable. "So they're primary sources," she said. "A primary source was produced at the time being studied, like a letter or a diary. My sister drilled it into me before her exams."

"And the exhibit over there," Claire said slowly, "the panel by the case, the one about the town during the war. That came later. Somebody wrote that by reading letters like these and putting a story on top of them."

"Textbook stuff," Priya said. "Somebody's interpretation."

Claire stood, crossed to the exhibit case, and read the panel again with new eyes. It cited the strike, briefly, and called the workers disaffected, a single confident adjective doing the work of a hundred unrecorded conversations. She came back and laid her uncle's version, the exhibit's version, and the letters themselves on the table like three overlapping photographs of the same street. The letters were closest to the event, and they were also patchy, cranky, half about shoes. The exhibit was clear and tidy and written by someone who had never smelled the rain of October 1944. Neither one was false. Both were partial. She had wanted the past to hand her a verdict, and instead it had handed her an afternoon of small, contradictory human weather.

She started sorting anyway, not for proof now but for pattern, stacking the letters that mentioned the plant to one side. Priya pulled up a chair and took a bundle, reading dates aloud. "This one's December. She says the men came back to the line after three days." Three days, Claire thought, not the long bitter standoff of the family legend. Or maybe three days at that plant, and longer somewhere she knew nothing about. She wrote both possibilities in her notebook, side by side, and did not cross either out.

"I can't decide," she said. "I've got the essay due and I can't decide what happened."

"Then say that," Priya said, still reading. "Say the sources don't agree and the question you're asking isn't the question they were answering. That's a real essay."

Claire laughed, surprising herself, and the sound didn't quite assuage the frustration but loosened it enough that she could keep working. She picked up the next letter, and at the bottom of the page, under her grandmother's careful closing, she found a postscript she hadn't noticed: Thomas got his shift back, and don't tell his mother he lost it at all.

Claire read it twice, then turned the letter toward Priya without a word.

story:
The folding tables had been set up along one side of the parking lot, and by ten the whole operation had settled into its diurnal rhythm: cars easing up the driveway, trunks opening, boxes carried to the sorting station where Amy stood with a clipboard she did not yet know how to use. She had signed up two weeks ago, mostly because the form was online and the online form was easy, and because her mother had said it would look good, though her mother had also said, in the same breath, that looking good was a terrible reason to do anything, which left Amy somewhere in the middle, holding both ideas at once.

Her trainer was a college sophomore named Priya who wore a laminated badge and spoke in the clipped, friendly cadence of someone who had answered the same questions many times. "Canned goods, unopened dry goods, anything still sealed," Priya said, tapping the edge of a crate. "If it's opened, or if someone made it at home, we can't take it. We can't check how it was prepared or stored." She said this the way a person recites a phone number, and moved on to the expiration dates.

Amy began sorting. It was simpler than she had imagined, and stranger. A can of pears passed through her hands, then a sack of rice with a torn corner, which went into the discard bin, then a jar of honey so old the label had faded to the color of weak tea. Somewhere behind her, a man was arguing gently about a box of dented soup, and a toddler was conducting a diurnal investigation of the curb, putting one pebble after another into his pocket. The morning had the feeling of a machine with soft edges.

The woman arrived at eleven, holding a foil pan with both arms the way people carry sleeping infants. She was small, gray-haired, wearing a church nametag that said Dora, and she set the pan on the end of Amy's table with evident ceremony. "Lasagna," she said. "Six of them back at home, still warm. We had a fundraiser dinner last night and nobody ate the lasagna. They all wanted the fried chicken."

Amy looked at the foil, at the little bead of sauce that had escaped one corner, at Dora's face, which was expecting a particular answer. She remembered Priya's sentence. She tried to soften it and found that softening it made it longer, so she went back to the short version. "I'm so sorry, we can't take home-cooked or opened food. We can't check how it was prepared or stored." The words felt borrowed, like singing harmony on a song she'd only heard once.

Dora demurred. She lifted the foil to show Amy the neat rectangles beneath, as if visibility were the issue, and said that she had been cooking for fifty years and had never once made anyone sick, and that her own mother had run the food pantry in Marion and would be ashamed, honestly, ashamed. Amy did not argue. She said the lasagna looked beautiful, and it did, and she said the rule was not about Dora, which she believed, and then she asked whether the church had a shelter they could take it to instead, since shelters, she had heard, could sometimes serve fresh food directly.

That last part she invented on the spot, or half-invented, and she flagged it to Dora as a guess rather than a fact, which seemed to matter to Dora more than the refusal had. "My nephew runs the warming center over on Francis Street," Dora said slowly, recalculating. "They'd eat it tonight." She picked up the pan. Before she left she touched the table with two fingers, a small blessing or a small goodbye, and Amy watched her carry the lasagna toward a sedan parked in the shade, still warm, still six pans deep in a kitchen somewhere.

Later, stacking cans of beans into a pyramid that kept slumping, Amy turned the morning over without settling it. The rule was sound, she thought; she understood why a pantry handing food to strangers had to know its history, and she would say the same sentence tomorrow if someone brought a casserole. And still, Dora standing there with her foil pan had been right about something too, that food made by a person for other persons is not the same as food that has merely survived its packaging. Both things were true and they pressed against each other like the two rows of cans she was trying to balance. Priya passed with an empty crate and asked how the first shift was going. "Complicated," Amy said, and Priya laughed and said wait until the pallet of oatmeal comes.

story:
James arrived at the loading dock at eight in the morning with his mother's gardening gloves in his backpack, because the email had said something about a community garden, and he had imagined himself weeding between tomatoes. Instead a woman named Rosa handed him a box cutter and pointed at a trailer half full of dented cans. "Sort the damaged from the good," she said. "Labels facing up. We're behind."

He worked beside a man in his sixties called Wendell, who had been coming every Saturday for three years and who narrated the morning like a radio announcer with a sardonic streak, remarking on the quality of the donated green beans, on the driver who was always late, on the weather, which he claimed to hold personally against the previous mayor. James laughed at the right pauses. He was good at that, the way he was good at class discussions, offering a sentence that sounded considered without committing him to anything.

What he kept noticing, though, was the silence of the place. The warehouse was enormous, steel shelving reaching up into shadow, forklifts beeping somewhere in the aisles, and yet no one came in asking for food. Not one person all morning. He had assumed, when he signed up, that he would be handing bags of groceries to people who needed them, that he would see the point of his labor in someone's face. Instead he moved boxes from pallet A to pallet B, and the boxes left on a truck, and that was all.

"Where does everybody go?" he finally asked Wendell, wiping his hands on his jeans. "The people who need this. Nobody's walked in all day."

Wendell looked at him for a second, then let out a short laugh that wasn't unkind. "This is the food bank," he said. "It's a warehouse. It collects everything and ships it out to the churches and the schools, all the little local agencies. The place where people actually pick up their groceries is called a pantry. Different building, over on Miller Street. You want faces, you signed up at the wrong address."

James felt his face warm. In his head he had already written the college application paragraph, the one about giving back, and now the paragraph looked thin, a performance for an audience that never arrived. He asked Rosa about it during the lunch break, sitting on an overturned milk crate, and she nodded. "People get that mixed up all the time," she said. "Half our new volunteers expect a line out the door. But we're the middle of it. The agencies couldn't run without us, and we couldn't run without them."

That afternoon James rode his bike the six blocks to Miller Street, mostly because he didn't want to go home and admit the day had confused him. The pantry occupied the basement of a church, and there was, in fact, a line out the door. He watched a woman with two kids choose between pasta and rice with the seriousness of someone balancing a ledger, and a teenage girl from his own school, he realized with a small shock, signing in at a clipboard table. He looked away before she could see him, then felt ashamed of looking away, then made himself look back. She was gone.

Back in the warehouse on Monday, he had volunteered to come again, he found himself defending the warehouse against Wendell's complaining, which had turned political. Wendell had decided that the whole system was a scam run by people who liked feeling generous, and he made a speech about politicians, using the word populist twice, once as a compliment and once as an insult, in a way that seemed to James to cancel itself out. "You can't impugn Rosa's motives just because the system's ugly," James said, surprising himself with the firmness of it. "The food got here. It'll get there. Somebody has to move the boxes."

"Look at you," Wendell said, but he said it quietly, and he went back to sorting.

James didn't think he had solved anything. The girl from his school had seen him at a pantry and he hadn't said hello; he had spent a whole day working hard for people he would never see, and it was good work or it was easy work or it was both; the line at Miller Street and the silence of the warehouse were the same fact in two rooms, and he could hold them together without pretending one canceled the other. What he could not yet decide was whether that was enough, or whether enough was even the right question, or whether questions like that were just another way of standing outside. He finished the pallet, tore down the empty boxes, and stacked the flattened cardboard against the wall until Rosa called from the office that the truck was early. He picked up the box cutter and went to meet it.

story:
The gray looked warm on the left side of the canvas and cool on the right, and Kaitlyn had mixed both patches from the same cup. She sat with her brush above the paper, checking the cup, checking the canvas, checking the cup again. Around her the craft shed smelled of cedar shavings and turpentine, and through the open door she could see the lake, flat and white at noon, and the dock where the younger campers were lined up for swim check. Mrs. Okafor had said the pieces were due on the porch by four o'clock Friday, hung and labeled, for the parents' visiting day. That gave Kaitlyn two afternoons, and she had spent the first one painting a sky that refused to be one color.

"Your gray is doing something weird," said Dana, leaning over from the next stool. Dana was painting a frog, which was not the assignment, but nobody had impugned her choice yet, least of all Kaitlyn, who admired people who could ignore instructions without visible anxiety.

"It's the same gray," Kaitlyn said. "I mixed it once. I've been using one cup."

"Then your eyes are broken." Dana held her own brush up like a thermometer. "Left side it looks like it wants to be brown. Right side it wants to be blue."

Kaitlyn laid a strip of the gray on a clean scrap of white paper, and there, alone, it was neither warm nor cool, just gray, a plain honest gray. She set the scrap beside the canvas, beside the orange she had laid down for a sunset below the sky, and beside the green she'd used for the far shore. Against the orange the gray bent warm. Against the green it bent cool. She moved the scrap back and forth like a card trick, watching the color slide, and felt the particular pleasure of a problem turning from an accident into a law. Something was happening that had rules, which meant something had written the rules down, somewhere, in a book, before she was born.

From her stool, Dana watched this happen with the patience of someone waiting for a kettle. She had known Kaitlyn for six weeks of canoe trips and dish duty, long enough to recognize the stillness that came over her when she stopped painting and started hunting. Dana herself worked the other way, piling paint on and hoping; but she liked watching Kaitlyn corner an idea, the way she liked watching the counselors try to fix the leaky craft-shed roof with a confidence neither of them had earned. Kaitlyn got up without a word and went to the shelf by the window where somebody's donated books were stacked between the jars of brushes, books with swollen covers and water stains shaped like continents.

The book she wanted was not there, but an older one was, a paint manual with a cracked spine, and in its index she found a line that stopped her: Chevreul, 1839. She read the page twice. The chemist Michel Eugène Chevreul had published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839, describing how a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it. She said it under her breath, then out loud, because Dana was watching.

"The law of simultaneous contrast," Kaitlyn said. "That's what he called it. Complements. Orange and blue, green and red. The gray shifts toward whatever's opposite its neighbor."

"So your sky is a science experiment now."

"My sky was always a science experiment. I just didn't know I was running it."

She went back to the canvas with the scrap of gray still in her hand. The problem, once she understood it, got larger rather than smaller. If the gray changed depending on what touched it, then she could not paint a neutral sky at all; she could only paint a sky that behaved differently in every region, warm over the sunset, cool over the pines. Part of her wanted to fight that, to isolate the gray, to give every patch its own border of white so it would hold still. Another part of her, a newer part, wanted the opposite: to choose the neighbors on purpose, so the gray would turn warm exactly where she wanted warmth, without her ever dipping the brush in anything but the one cup. It seemed almost like cheating, and also like the most honest thing available, and she could not fully decide which, so she sat with both ideas while the swim-check line on the dock moved one camper at a time into the water and out again.

Mrs. Okafor came through at three to count finished pieces, tapping her clipboard against her palm. "Friday at four," she said, stopping at Kaitlyn's table. "Not Friday at five. Not Saturday morning while the cars are loading." She looked at the half-sky for a long moment. "What you have there is either unfinished or very subtle, and I can't tell which."

"Neither can I," Kaitlyn said, which was truer than she meant it to be.

On Friday she hung the painting with a label card that read, in her small careful hand, Kaitlyn, age 16, sky in one gray, and stood back beside Dana while the first parents came up the path. The gray lay warm and cool in bands above the sunset and above the painted shore, doing both things at once, and she watched a woman in a sun hat lean in close, tilt her head, and touch the canvas frame as if checking it for heat.

story:
The receipt printer at Pemberton Hardware jammed whenever the air conditioning was off, so Alexis had learned to read the tape as it emerged, line by line, like a telegram. Pipe fitting, 6.49. Pipe fitting, 6.49. GST, 0.65. She was seventeen and had been working the counter since June, and it was the GST line that bothered her, because she could not make it come out right. Seven percent of 12.98 was 0.91, not 0.65, and either the machine was broken or she was.

She asked her uncle Ray at Sunday dinner, since he had owned a body shop since before she was born and claimed to know everything the government did to a person. "Seven percent," he said, with the certainty of a man who had not looked at a receipt in years. "It's the Goods and Services Tax. Came in when I was your age. Seven percent, and they swore it would never go up." Alexis wrote it in her phone under a note titled Things To Verify, which also contained the boiling point of castor oil and the name of the boy who had painted the mural behind the arena.

The following Thursday her father asked her to come along to the accountant's office, partly because he liked the company and partly because she was his witness now that her mother refused to attend anything involving the word remittance. Alexis brought the crumpled receipt in her jacket pocket. She also brought her own paycheque stub, her first from the hardware store, which she had examined on the bus until the numbers felt like a riddle: gross pay 612.00, then a staircase of subtractions, then net pay 549.33. Someone was taking money out before the money reached her, and the stub named them all in a small, patient font.

The accountant's office was above a florist's and smelled faintly of lilies and toner. Mr. Okafor had a desk with two monitors and a jar of liquorice allsorts he offered to visitors and never ate himself. He and Alexis's father went through the tax return like men walking a familiar field, checking fences. Employment income. Union dues. The deduction for the safety boots her father had bought in March, which reduced the income he was taxed on rather than the tax itself, a distinction Alexis found slippery until Mr. Okafor held up the boot receipt and said, "This makes your income smaller on paper. The tax man taxes the smaller number." Her father said that seemed fair, in the tone of a man who did not quite believe it.

Alexis had been waiting for a gap, and there was one while her father went downstairs to feed the parking meter with coins he counted like a gambler. She flattened the hardware receipt on the desk. "Can I ask something that isn't about us," she said. "The GST on this. It's five percent, isn't it. I checked the arithmetic four times." Mr. Okafor turned the receipt toward himself without hurry. "Five percent," he said. "It was seven when it started, on the first of January, 1991. It's been five percent since the first of January, 2008."

She absorbed this the way you absorb news that a relative has been remarried for years. Her uncle had been so sure. She thought of her math teacher, Mr. Delgado, who called a small proven fact a lemma, a stepping stone you built on your way to the theorem you actually wanted, and she thought that uncle Ray's seven percent had been a lemma built on sand. "So my uncle's wrong," she said. "Not wrong about his whole life," said Mr. Okafor. "Just behind it by a while." He pulled a liquorice allsort from the jar, looked at it, and put it back.

From where he sat, Marcus Okafor could see the girl doing arithmetic in her head, her lips moving slightly, the way his daughter did when calculating whether she could afford both the sneakers and the concert. He had learned, over nineteen tax seasons, that the ones who asked about the GST line at seventeen either became accountants or became the kind of citizens who read their mail, and both were fine outcomes. Her father came back up the stairs with a sullen expression about the meter, having fed it four dollars for forty minutes, and the return resumed.

But Alexis kept returning to her paycheque stub, which she unfolded now and laid beside the receipt. "So the GST is me paying tax when I spend," she said slowly, "and these are tax taken out when I earn. Both at once. I'm taxed going in and coming out." Mr. Okafor considered whether to correct her and decided she had earned the simplification. "More or less," he said. "Though the return exists because we guess wrong in both directions. Sometimes you've paid too much through the year and they owe you. Sometimes not." Alexis looked at the stub's patient little font, at the deductions that had been taken from her as though she were an established person with obligations, and felt something complicated that she did not yet have a word for. Pride, possibly. Or indignation. They sat close together.

Her father signed the return in three places, each signature smaller than the last, as though the pen itself were being taxed. "Will we get money back?" Alexis asked. "We'll see," her father said, which was his answer to everything from refunds to weather.

On the bus home, Alexis texted her uncle: it's 5 percent now, it changed in 2008, it started at 7 in 1991. Three dots appeared, hovered, and vanished. She put the phone away and took out the receipt one more time, running her thumb over the small grey line, GST 0.65, correct and certain and printed twice because the machine had jammed.

story:
The queue at the phone store moved slowly enough that Samantha had time to read the posters twice. One promised a free phone with a two-year plan, the word free set in type so confident it seemed to presage a world where nothing was paid for, ever. She clutched the paper sleeve of her broken handset, which had died in a puddle outside her internship two days before, and rehearsed what she would say: she needed something cheap, something that would last until September, when college began and everything was supposed to become clearer.

"Next." The clerk was younger than Samantha expected, maybe twenty, with the patient ascetic air of someone who had explained the same three plans a thousand times and had stopped expecting anyone to understand them. He slid a folder across the counter and uncapped a pen. "Just need your signature here, here, and initials there. It's the standard agreement."

"Can I read it?" she asked.

He blinked, then recovered. "Sure. Nobody does, but sure." He stepped away to help a man comparing screen protectors, and Samantha bent over the pages. The first was dense with language she half recognized from movies: terms and conditions, liability, limitation thereof, the company shall not be held responsible. Further down, the word consent appeared in a paragraph about data sharing, and she realized she was being asked to agree to things she had not known existed an hour ago.

Her phone buzzed, which was impossible, and she flinched before remembering the clerk's loaner on the counter. It was her friend Dana, and the message brought the old argument back whole: Marcus still hadn't paid the fifty dollars he'd promised for a month of calculus tutoring in the spring. Dana insisted a deal was a deal. Marcus had laughed and said, "It's not like we signed anything," and Samantha had let it go because finals were coming and the money felt somehow unimportant next to the physics exam. Now, reading a document whose entire power seemed to live in a signature, she wondered what exactly a signature did.

The man at the screen protector counter was speaking loudly into his own phone, and she caught fragments without meaning to. "No, look, I'm telling you, there's no contract there. A contract needs an offer, an acceptance, and consideration, meaning something of value given by each side in exchange." Samantha's eyes lifted from the page. "You offered to pay him, he tutored you, that's the something of value from each side," the man said. "The writing doesn't matter. Tell him that."

She looked back down at the folder. The free phone, she now saw, was folded into the plan as a monthly credit; the plan itself cost more per month than the cheaper one without a phone. The free thing was the expensive thing wearing a costume. And the early termination fee, buried two pages in under a heading about liability, was two hundred dollars. She thought of Marcus's fifty dollars and felt an odd double movement in herself: she had been on his side because he was funny and the debt was informal, and she was on the store's side because the folder was formal, and both positions had rested on the same lazy assumption, that seriousness lived in paperwork. Apparently it did not. Apparently Dana had been right for a reason Samantha hadn't understood until a stranger's phone call drifted over a counter.

"Ready?" the clerk had returned.

"Almost." She read the termination clause a second time, slowly, letting the sentence about the two hundred dollars sit in her like a bruise she was choosing to accept or not accept. College was four years, not two. The plan would hold her longer than the phone would survive; screens met puddles, her whole recent history proved that. But her mother had wired her three hundred dollars that morning, the last gift before the declared end of parental subsidies, and the idea of losing two hundred of it to a broken screen in October felt genuinely deleterious, not abstractly but in meals.

"Question," she said. "If I take the smaller plan and buy the phone outright, is that the same total?"

He tapped his screen, and his eyebrows moved a millimeter, which from him was practically astonishment. "It's forty dollars less. But you'd pay the phone up front today."

"Then that one." She signed the shorter form, once, where the arrow indicated, and her signature came out smaller than she expected, as though her hand understood before she did that this was the version she meant. She slid the pen back and pocketed the loaner. Outside, she stopped on the curb and texted Dana: "You were right about Marcus. Tell him it counts even without a signature. I'll explain tonight."

"Explain what?" Dana wrote back.

"The thing somebody said in line at the phone store," Samantha typed, then deleted it, then wrote, "His fifty dollars. I'm collecting it, and he's paying it."

Nicolas had a list on his phone and a mission in his pocket, and the mission was this: cook dinner for his family before his mother got home at seven, and cook it well, because tonight was the night he proved he could be trusted with the kitchen. The farmers' market occupied two rows of white tents in the gravel lot by the river, and the morning smelled like roasted chiles and wet lettuce. At five thousand feet above the sea, the town sat high enough that the light came down thin and bright, and Nicolas felt efficient just standing in it.

The trouble began, as troubles do, with memory. He wanted to make the pasta dish from the family's camping trip last month, the one his father had requested twice since. But that trip had produced a pot of noodles that were, in his sister Priya's verdict, "crunchy in a way pasta should never consent to be." He had boiled them for exactly the time on the box. Everyone had teased him for a full twenty minutes. Priya had announced she was drafting a formal complaint. Nicolas had told her she'd need a subpoena if she wanted him to testify about the water. He had laughed about it, then and now, but something about it still snagged, like a fact with a burr on it.

At the tomato stand, a girl about his age was arranging heirlooms with the seriousness of a museum curator. She was effusive about everything, every variety, every grower, every irrigation method, so much so that Nicolas briefly wondered if she was being paid by the adjective. "The Purple Cherokees," she said, holding one up like a jewel, "are the sweetest thing at this market, and I will defend that position against all rivals." He bought four.

"Can I ask you something weird," he said, bagging them. "You've lived here your whole life, right? Does pasta take longer to cook up here?"

"Pasta, rice, beans, eggs, everything boiled," she said. "The water boils cooler at this altitude. Around ninety-five degrees Celsius at five thousand feet, instead of a hundred. So things just take longer."

He stared at her. "The box said nine minutes."

"The box lives at sea level," she said, and turned to greet another customer, leaving Nicolas holding his tomatoes and his whole ruined alibi. It wasn't his fault. Or it was partly his fault, in the way that not knowing things is a kind of fault you can fix by finding out. On the camping trip, he had stood at the stove feeling like a failure while the altitude quietly sabotaged him, and Priya's complaint had been, technically, dismissed.

He stopped at the herb stand and then, because he was on a roll, at the egg stand, where the vendor's metal cashbox gave him a shock sharp enough to make him yelp. "Dry mountain air," the vendor said, not looking up. "It'll ionize everything you touch by October. Hair, sweaters, doorknobs. You get used to it or you get used to apologizing to cats." Nicolas rubbed his thumb and decided he would do neither, and also that he loved this market, where even the static electricity came with commentary.

At home he laid out his ingredients like evidence for a trial he now intended to win. Priya drifted into the kitchen around six, ostensibly for a glass of water, actually to supervise. "Is it the pasta again," she said. "Should I alert the authorities."

"The authorities have been consulted," Nicolas said. "The water boils at ninety-five degrees Celsius here, not a hundred, because of the altitude. So it's going to take longer, and I'm building that in. Eleven minutes, twelve, whatever it needs."

Priya leaned against the counter, watching him salt the water with the new confidence of a man who understood his enemy. "So you're saying the camping pasta wasn't your fault."

"I'm saying the mountain did it," Nicolas said. "I was an innocent bystander."

"You were the one holding the spoon."

"I was an innocent bystander holding a spoon, in a jurisdiction with compromised boiling." He stirred the sauce, tasting, adjusting, and Priya stole a piece of tomato off the cutting board and pronounced it, grudgingly, excellent.

He tasted a noodle at nine minutes, another at eleven, and at twelve and a half they gave, finally, in the way they were supposed to, soft all the way through without going limp. He fished one out for Priya without being asked. She chewed it slowly, like a judge who had been wrong before and knew the cost of ruling too fast. Their mother's car pulled into the driveway. Priya swallowed, looked at the pot, looked at him, and said, "Withdraw the complaint. Mostly."

story:
Ryan had told his father he would handle dinner, and his father had said fine, in the flat voice he had been using since March, since the plant cut its second shift and the house went quiet in the middle of the day. So Ryan stood in the kitchen on Sunday afternoon with flour on his forearms and a plan he had not entirely thought through: homemade bread, the kind his grandmother used to make, soup from a carton, a table that looked like somebody had tended it.

The recipe said to mix flour, water, yeast and salt, then knead for eight minutes. Eight minutes felt like a very long time when your hands kept sticking and the dough kept tearing, so he had stopped at maybe five, maybe less, shaped it into a round, and set it near the window to rise. His sister Delia came through for a glass of water and watched him hover over it. "You're staring at bread," she said. "It's not going to do tricks." But it did rise, slowly, a pale dome under a damp towel, and when he slashed the top with a knife and put it in the oven he felt something in his chest unclench for the first time in weeks.

The loaf came out looking right, golden and cracked along the cut, and it sounded hollow when he knocked on it, which the recipe said was good. But when he sawed off the end piece, the crumb was dense and close, almost crumbly, nothing like the open, springy interior of his grandmother's loaves. He pressed a piece between his fingers and it compressed and stayed compressed. He ate it anyway, standing at the counter, and it tasted like flour and salt and failure in roughly equal parts.

His father drifted in around five, saturnine as he'd been all spring, and looked at the loaf without comment. "It's the first one," Ryan said, more sharply than he meant, and his father held up both hands, palms out, the gesture of a man declining a fight he hadn't started. Delia, who could not bear a silence, said, "It's actually not bad with butter," which was kind of her and also a bit of a prevaricate, since she had eaten one piece and made a face at it when she thought no one was watching.

That night Ryan sat at the kitchen table with his phone and a library book Delia had brought home on a whim, a fat one about bread, its dust jacket long gone. He had assumed bread was mostly luck, or a talent some people had, but the book kept insisting on process. He read one sentence three times. "Gluten forms when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin mix with water," he said aloud, mostly to the empty room, "and kneading longer makes the gluten network stronger and the bread chewier." Delia, passing through in pajamas, repeated "gliadin" twice as though tasting it, then said he'd better not become one of those people with a starter in the fridge named after a dead poet, and went upstairs.

So the crumbly loaf had been his fault in a way he could name. Five minutes of kneading had not been enough to build whatever glutenin and gliadin built when water got involved, and the network inside his dough had stayed weak, and the bread had come out dense because there was nothing strong enough inside it to hold it open. He didn't know whether that was the whole story, whether the water had been off or the yeast tired, and the book admitted that bread kept its own accounts. But the kneading part was something he could control, and he decided that was worth more than knowing everything.

He started the second loaf at seven the next morning, before anyone else was up. This time he set a timer and kneaded the full eight minutes, then kept going, folding the dough over itself, pushing with the heel of his hand, turning the bowl a quarter turn, over and over, until his shoulders burned and the dough stopped tearing and began to stretch, smooth as an earlobe, a veneer of satin on its surface where the shaggy roughness had been. It was strange to think that the change was happening at a level he couldn't see, proteins linking hands underwater, and stranger still that his tired arms were the instrument of it.

The second loaf rose higher and faster, as though the dough had been waiting for permission. When it came out of the oven at noon, his father was at the table with the job listings spread in front of him, and Delia was eating cereal, and Ryan set the loaf down on a rack without a word. He let it cool as long as he could stand, which was not entirely, and cut it. The crumb tore open, soft and full of irregular holes, and when he pulled a piece it stretched before it gave.

"Chewy," Delia said, with her mouth full, in a tone that suggested she was surprised to be issuing a compliment. His father put down the listings, tore a piece from the heel, and chewed it slowly, looking at the window, and then at his son's flour-dusted shirt, and then back at the window. "Save me another slice," he said. "I'll take it with the soup tonight."

The envelope had been in the bottom of Sophia's backpack since Tuesday, and by Friday morning she still had not opened it. It was thin, institutional, the kind that extruded envelopes by the thousand from some office on the second floor of the humanities building, and everyone in the economics elective knew what it probably was. Ms. Ferreira had announced on Monday that the summer research stipend decisions had gone out. Sophia had applied in October for the two-year track, the one that paid a hundred dollars more in the second summer but nothing the first. She had chosen it deliberately, back in October, and had felt principled about it, the way you feel principled about things that are far away.

At lunch Marcus slid his tray across from hers without asking, which was how they always sat. He was eating with the grim discipline of an ascetic, plain rice, plain chicken, because he was saving for a camera lens, and he wanted to talk about the study the psych students were running in the library for course credit. "It's those questions about money," he said. "Would you rather have fifty now or a hundred in a year. Then they ask you again with years added on. It took ten minutes and I got a granola bar."

"And you said?"

"Fifty now, obviously. I'm not waiting a year for anything." He shoveled rice. "Except the weird part is, for the far ones I picked the hundred. A hundred in six years over fifty in five. Six years, man. Who cares." He said the researcher had a word for it, something clinical, and Sophia said she didn't want to know the word yet, and he shrugged and moved on to the lens, which was $340, which was why he was eating like a monk and why he had, last week, sold his concert ticket to Devon for $50 cash.

That was the offer on the table, actually, still technically on the table. Devon had a job now and wanted to buy the ticket back, and he had told Sophia, because she'd been saving for the same summer program's materials fee, that he'd front her the money today. Fifty dollars, today, for the sketch supplies she'd need if she got the one-year track. Or she could hold out, decline Devon, wait on the envelope, and if it was the two-year track take the larger amount later. She had watched herself in October pick the patient option without even hesitating. She had also, this morning, watched her hand start toward texting Devon yes before she put the phone face down on the lab table.

She opened the envelope fifth period, in the stairwell by the chemistry rooms where nobody went. The air smelled like the tar the roofers had been heating all week, and below her, through the door, she could hear Mr. Okonkwo's voice droning through molarity. She slid her thumb under the flap.

Two-year track. Confirmed. $100 the second summer, nothing the first. She read it twice. Then she stood very still, because a fact she had been refusing to look at all week was suddenly standing in front of her with its hands out. She had chosen the hundred, waiting two whole years for it, and it had cost her nothing to choose, because six years or five years or two years versus one, the distance made the patience easy. But today, with Devon's fifty dollars real and immediate, her whole body had leaned toward it. Same girl. Same arithmetic. Two different answers depending on how close the money stood.

She found Marcus after last bell by the vending machines, feeding quarters into the slot with his rice-survivor expression. "That word," she said. "From the study." He looked at her, then at the machine as it clunked and withheld his chips. "Present bias," he said, and hit the glass with the flat of his hand. "That's what they called it."

Sophia leaned against the machine. She told him the whole shape of it, the two-year stipend, the October version of herself who had been so serene about waiting, the fifty dollars she'd nearly taken this morning because it was today and her sketch paper was today and the fee was due Monday. "The far choice I made like it was nothing," she said. "The near one, I couldn't even feel my own principles." She didn't pretend it was solved. She still needed supplies by Monday, and the patient track still paid nothing for a year, and no insight changed either of those facts. What she had was smaller: she could see the seam now, where her October self and her Friday self disagreed, and she could refuse to pretend they were the same person by accident.

Marcus retrieved his chips at last, handed them to her without ceremony, and told her Devon was still in the weight room if she wanted the fifty. Sophia took out her phone. She typed a message to Devon, deleted it, typed another. Then she put the phone away and walked down the hall toward the art room, because Mrs. Lantz kept a cabinet of donated supplies that nobody had inventoried since September, and she wanted to see what was in it before she decided anything. The door was locked, but the art room had a second entrance through the kiln room, and the kiln room door was always open. She pushed through it into the warm clay-smelling dark, her hand finding the light switch by feel.

Kaitlyn had told herself the plan so many times that afternoon that it had started to feel like a memory instead of a choice: meet Marcus at the fountain by the food court at four, wander the mall, eat pretzels, and be home by seven because her mother, who trusted her exactly as far as the parking lot, would be waiting in the car. She had also told herself that she looked calm, which was true only if you didn't count her hands.

She got there early, which she did not do, and stood outside the aquarium shop watching a tank of clownfish weave through anemones. A plaque said the arrangement was called mutualism, both creatures getting something from the deal. That was the thing about Marcus, she'd decided. They were good for each other. He'd helped her monetize the vintage-clothing account she ran by suggesting she photograph the good jackets flat-laid on white, and sales had doubled. She was good for him too, though she couldn't have said how, exactly, and decided not to examine it.

"You're already here," Marcus said, arriving at 4:02 with his skateboard under his arm like a coat rack had followed him in from the sidewalk. "I was going to be the early one."

"I was passing," she said, which was a lie, since the mall was a forty-minute bus ride from her house and she had tried on three shirts before noon.

They walked. That was the whole activity, walking, and it turned out to be enough. They went into the bookstore and read each other the worst lines from romance novels in the aisles. They rated the smell of every candle in the home store, and Marcus gave one called Seaside Dawn a four because, he said, the real thing at the littoral edge where the tide pulled back smelled more like salt and rotting kelp, and she believed him, because he actually went to the shore and paid attention to it, which seemed like a reason to like someone more than any shirt she'd tried on that morning.

By the time they bought the pretzels, she had revised her account of the evening several times, and each version was more confident than the last. In the current draft, they were already basically together, and the only remaining question was how the night would end, which she had also drafted. He'd walk her to her mother's car. Something would happen at the door, probably, or maybe just outside the mall doors where the evening light came through the glass all long and gold.

Then, on the walk toward the exit, he slowed down near the fountain and said, "Hey, can I say something weird."

"Is it about the pretzel? Because I know I got cinnamon sugar on your sleeve."

"No. It's that I told my brother this was a date, and you told Priya it was hanging out, and I don't actually know which one we're doing, and either one is fine, but I'd rather know than guess." He turned the bracelet on his wrist twice around his finger, the way he did when he'd decided something.

Kaitlyn stood very still next to the fountain, where the coins of a hundred other wishes sat green underwater. She had said it was hanging out to Priya. She had said it to protect herself, in case it went badly, so she could claim nothing had been at stake, and only now, with the evidence in the open, did that look less like protection and more like a locked door. "It was a date," she said. "I said the other thing because I was scared you'd say it wasn't."

"Okay," Marcus said. "Good." And he smiled in a way that took the whole architecture of her drafted evening apart, gently, like taking out a pin.

They walked out through the big glass doors into the gold light she had predicted, and near the bench by the crosswalk he stopped again. "So I was going to maybe kiss you goodnight, and I told myself I would, but I think I'd rather just say goodnight instead. Is that okay? You can change your mind about stuff too, that's the whole point, you can even say yes and then take it back."

"Yeah," she said. "That's okay. You can take it back."

Her mother's car was idling under the lamp at the far end of the lot. Kaitlyn found that she was not disappointed, or not the way the drafted versions of her had been. Something had been offered and something had been declined and both of those things had been survivable, which was a kind of mutualism too, if she was honest, though she still didn't know what he got out of the arrangement, and might not for a while.

"Same time next Saturday," Marcus said, stepping back, skateboard up under his arm. "Actual date. You can wear the third shirt, the one you almost picked."

"You don't know about the shirts."

"Priya knows about the shirts," he said, and walked off toward his bus while she stood there deciding whether to be furious at Priya or text her the entire evening immediately. She chose the second one, thumb already flying, and behind her the mall doors sighed open and shut on the smell of cinnamon sugar and cold salt air.

story:
Rose found the violin in her grandmother's hallway closet, behind a box of winter coats, and carried it to the kitchen table the way you carry something that might still be alive. Her grandmother looked up from the sink, dried her hands, and said only, "The E string is flat. It's been flat since 1987."

She had played clarinet for six years, sight-read anything put in front of her, and had assumed that reading notes was what playing an instrument meant. But the violin had no holes for her fingers, no keys, no map. Her grandmother tuned it for her, placed her fingers on the strings one afternoon, and then did something Rose didn't expect: she hummed a phrase from an old folk song and said, "Now play that back." When Rose asked for the sheet music, her grandmother laughed. "I never had any. There wasn't any in the house."

The problem arrived on Saturday in the form of Birdie, nine years old, who lived two farms over and took the bus to the house every week for a lesson her grandmother gave for nothing. Rose thought that was altruistic of her, though she also suspected her grandmother simply liked the company. Birdie could play. That was the humiliating part. She set her small violin under her chin and produced a clean, singing "Go Tell Aunt Rhody" while Rose stood in the doorway holding the sheet music she had transcribed the night before, her version of being prepared.

"You read it off the paper," Birdie said afterward, squinting at Rose's pages. "What are all those flags for?" She genuinely didn't know. She could play a dozen songs and could not name a single note on the staff. Rose felt something twist that wasn't quite contempt and wasn't quite envy, some hybrid she couldn't file. She had spent years building a system of reading, and here was a child who bypassed it entirely, the way, Rose thought and then stopped thinking, a toddler talks long before anyone hands it an alphabet.

She cornered her grandmother at the kitchen table that evening, the fact sheets spread out. "How does she do that without reading?"

"It's how she was taught. The Suzuki method. Shinichi Suzuki, the Japanese violinist. He started children playing by ear before they ever read music, the way they learn to speak before they learn to read."

"Then she's missing half of it," Rose said.

"Or you are."

They did not settle it. Rose went to bed angry in the clean, useless way that keeps you awake counting ceiling cracks. In the morning she found Birdie on the porch steps sawing through "Twinkle, Twinkle" and sat down beside her with the transcript. "Trade," Rose said. "You teach me the song by ear. I teach you the notes." Birdie considered this with the gravity of a customs officer. "You have to promise not to abrogate," she said, and Rose, who had taught her that word two days earlier from a crossword, promised not to abrogate.

The lesson was harder than either expected. Birdie could not understand why Rose kept stopping to look down at fingers that wouldn't obey, and Rose could not understand how Birdie's hands knew where to go without ever asking permission. "You just hear where it goes," Birdie said, and when Rose snapped that that wasn't an answer, Birdie played the next phrase wrong on purpose, so slowly that Rose could hear the right note arriving before Birdie's finger landed on it. Rose copied the correction. Then copied it again. On the fourth try the phrase came out whole, and she had not looked at the paper once.

Her grandmother came out with lemonade and the mail, and set down a postcard from the clinic reminding her that her allergy shots were due. "Antigens," she said vaguely, reading it, "little troublemakers they inject so your body learns the tune." Rose thought about that longer than the postcard deserved. A small dose of the thing that hurts, given on purpose, so the system learns to answer it.

She didn't conclude anything tidy. Some days she still believed reading was the spine of music and Birdie was a trick pony; other days, playing "Aunt Rhody" in the dark barn with her eyes shut, she believed the opposite. She decided she was allowed to hold both. On the last night of the visit she played the folk song through, twice, no music stand, and her grandmother called from the kitchen, "The E string's still flat."

"I know," Rose called back. "I like it now."
