Laurence found him at the third row of the bleachers, holding two cups of hot chocolate even though the game wouldn't start for twenty minutes, and she understood immediately that he had been worried about the same thing she had been worried about, which was having nothing to do with his hands. "I didn't know if you liked it," Dev said, offering one cup. "I guessed. Sugar's in the packet, not the cup, because I read once that people are particular." She took it. The night had that September smell of cut grass and cigarette smoke drifting from the parking lot, and the floodlights turned everyone's faces the same flat orange, which felt merciful, since it hid whatever her face was doing.

She had spent the drive here composing herself into someone blasé, a girl who watched football with mild amusement, who laughed at the right moments without investing anything, and the plan had already failed in the parking lot when she'd tripped on a chain and he'd caught her elbow and she'd said thank you twice, the second thank you quieter, as though the first had been a mistake. Now she sipped the hot chocolate and it was good, actually good, and she resented that, because it was harder to be cool about something good.

The marching band came out and scattered across the field like an archipelago, each cluster of brass and drums its own small island of noise. Dev leaned toward her to be heard over the drums. "You know my sister's in the clarinet section? Third row. She's been talking about this game for two weeks." He pointed, and there was a small wave from a girl in a green uniform, and Laurence waved back, and something about the wave, its unembarrassed eagerness, made her like him more, which she filed away as information she would examine later, alone.

By halftime she had accumulated a list of failures she kept without wanting to. She had misheard his joke about the referee and laughed two beats late. She had talked for what felt like four straight minutes about her intended major, urban studies, and had used the word "problematize" out loud, in a sentence, at a football game, and watched his expression go politely blank. When he'd asked whether she wanted a soft pretzel, she'd said "I'm good" in a tone that must have sounded like rejection of the entire category of pretzels, of shared food, possibly of him. The score was 21 to 14 and she could not have told you who was winning.

When the third quarter ended, Dev's phone buzzed and he looked at it too long. "My mom," he said. "She wants me home by eleven, she's, my grandpa's visiting and she wants the car in the driveway before he wakes up, he sleeps weird hours." He stood there holding the phone, not moving, and then he said, "I'm sorry. I know this is the worst possible timing. This was really..." He stopped, restarted. "I don't want to go."

Laurence walked him to the gate because it seemed like the thing a person would do, and the whole way she was composing the post-mortem: he couldn't even wait through the fourth quarter, he stood there struggling to say the date was anything at all. At the gate he turned around. "Can I be honest about something?" he said. "I've spent the entire game thinking you were bored. Like you came because your friend Priya said I was nice and now you're stuck here until the clock runs out. You kept looking at the field instead of at me, so I figured the field was more interesting, which, fair, but." He pushed his hands into his jacket pockets. "I kept trying to think of a way to ask if you were hating it without asking if you were hating it."

She stood there with her cup going cold in her hands. The field, the band, the whole roaring stadium was behind her, and she had been looking at it because looking at him was too much, and it had never once occurred to her that the direction of her eyes might have been read as a verdict on him. "I looked something up before tonight," she said. "Because I do that, I look things up, I looked up what to expect on first dates. There's this thing where after a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them. And how much they enjoyed their company. Both of those, it's the whole finding." She heard herself speeding up and made herself slow down. "It's called the liking gap. People walk away from first conversations and the other person liked them more than they think. That's what the study said."

"So you're saying," Dev said, "that I've been sitting there thinking you hated me, and you've been sitting there thinking I hated you, and we were both, statistically." He laughed, and she laughed, and then he wasn't laughing anymore, he was saying, "Text me when you get home, okay, not because I'm worried, just because I want to know," and then he jogged toward the parking lot, one hand raised, and she stood at the gate in the floodlight noise and took out her phone and typed, before she could curate it, "I did not hate a single minute."

story:
The used car lot sat behind the school like an archipelago of metal islands, and every afternoon David cut through it on his way home, slowing past the blue sedan with the faded FOR SALE sign in the window. He had two thousand dollars saved from three summers of mowing lawns, and his mother had promised, quietly, in the kitchen, that if he could cover half, she would help with the rest. The sedan was six thousand. The math felt possible in a way that made his chest tighten.

In geology that spring they had been forced to memorize rock types, and Mr. Okafor had passed around a chunk of obsidian, black and glassy, an igneous stone born from cooling lava. David had held it longer than he needed to. His grandfather had kept a chunk like it on his dresser, next to a savings passbook, and David remembered being nine, sitting on the bed's edge while the old man showed him the small deposits and the tiny sums the bank added each year, unearned, arriving like weather. "Money that sits still can grow," his grandfather had said, tapping the booklet, and David had believed it the way children believe things, without mechanism, without question.

Then the letter came. It was addressed to his mother, from the credit union, and she left it open on the counter while she made dinner, so David read it standing up, a spoon in his hand. The savings account had earned four percent last year; the balance, which had dipped after his father left, was climbing again, dollar by patient dollar. His mother watched him read it over his shoulder. "Grandpa would like that," she said, and handed him the carrots to peel.

At the dealership on Saturday, the salesman was a big, warm man named Ruiz who called David "young man" and his mother "ma'am" and brought them bottled water without being asked. The blue sedan was there, freshly washed. Six thousand dollars, Ruiz said, or they could finance it. He slid a paper across the desk: seventy-two months, one hundred and five a month. His mother's shoulders dropped a little with relief. David knew what her paycheck looked like; he knew one hundred and five was almost possible and one hundred and sixty was not.

"Or forty-eight months," Ruiz said, tapping another column, "but that's one thirty-five." David took the pen and added down both columns, twice, because the first answer seemed wrong. Forty-eight months at one thirty-five came to six thousand four hundred eighty. Seventy-two months at one hundred and five came to seven thousand five hundred sixty. He showed his mother the two totals. "The longer one has the smaller payment," he said slowly, working it out as he spoke, "but it costs more in the end. Like more than a thousand dollars more." Ruiz didn't argue. He looked at the paper, then at David, and something in his face shifted, less salesman, more uncle. "That's true," he said. "That's just how it works. At the same rate, more months means more interest over the life of the loan."

His mother was quiet in the car afterward. "We could do the four years," she said. "Tight, but maybe." Then, half a block on, the twist of the afternoon: Ruiz came jogging out of the lot with his jacket unbuttoned and caught them at the light. He handed David a card. "The sedan's owner trades with us," he said. "He'd probably take fifty-two hundred cash. No loan at all. I just thought somebody should mention it." He shrugged, embarrassed, and walked back before either of them could fully thank him.

David thought about it that night instead of homework. The cash offer would expropriate most of his savings in one gesture, the whole two thousand plus his mother's share, and the letter's patient four percent would have nothing left to work on. But no payment would arrive every month either, no stream of small subtractions, and his mother would keep her margins. He tried to hold both pictures at once: money growing because it sat still, and money spent because it moved something real into their driveway. He could not make the two pictures agree.

He texted his mother from bed: "We could pay cash and start saving again. Slower but no loan." She replied a minute later with a single thumbs up, then, after a longer pause: "Monday we offer 4900. If he says no, we do the 4 year loan. Deal?" David typed "deal," put the phone face down, and lay listening to the furnace tick. On Monday he would walk through the archipelago of cars one more time, and maybe drive one of them home.

Megan had chosen the bowling alley for practical reasons, which she could admit to herself but not to Dana, who was standing at the shoe counter holding size eights like they were evidence in a trial. If the date failed, a bowling alley offered exits: the arcade, the vending machine, the parking lot. If it succeeded, there were twelve frames in which to find out which kind of success it might be.

They had already done the coffee shop, an hour of small talk that Megan had tried twice to resuscitate with questions about siblings and weather and whether the barista had tattooed the words on her forearm or just Sharpied them. Dana had answered everything carefully, in complete sentences, and asked her almost nothing back. So when the silence had stretched to the point of embarrassment, Megan had reached for the one thing she'd been saving, the thing she'd read about at two in the morning instead of sleeping.

"There's this study," she'd said, stirring a coffee she no longer wanted. "Arthur Aron, 1997. Pairs of strangers took turns asking each other thirty-six questions that got gradually more personal, and they ended up feeling closer than pairs making small talk."

Dana had looked at her over the rim of the cup. "Closer than small talk. That's a low bar."

"It's a measurable bar. That's the point."

"So you want to run a psychology experiment on me."

"I want to bowl," Megan had said, standing up, "and ask you hard questions while we do it. You can ask me back."

Now, in the third frame, they were on question nine, which was the first one that had made Dana stop mid-approach and stand at the line with the ball held low, thinking. "If I could change one thing about the way I was raised," Dana repeated, "then what." The ball went into the gutter and neither of them mentioned it.

"For a long time I would have said nothing," Dana said, sitting down. "My parents would like that answer. It's the perspicacious answer, the one that makes you sound like you've thought everything through and arrived at gratitude." Megan watched her lace and unlace the fingers of the borrowed shoes. "But there was a year my mother didn't speak to my uncle, and nobody told me why, and I learned to stop asking why. I'd change that. The not asking."

Megan wrote her own answer to the same question on the back of the score sheet, folded it, and slid it across the ball return, which was their agreed system: answer for answer, no commentary until both were in. She bowled a spare while Dana read it. There was a consonance between them, she thought, in the way they both wrote small and fast, like they were afraid of being caught at it.

By the eighth frame they had reached the twenties, the questions she had privately doubted anyone would answer honestly. "When did you last cry in front of another person," she asked, and Dana said, "At my grandfather's funeral, but only because everyone else was crying and I was afraid of what it meant that I wasn't." Megan had a list of things she was afraid it meant too, and she said so, and Dana nodded like this was the most normal thing anyone had ever told her at lane fourteen.

The problem, Megan was beginning to understand, was that the questions were working, and she couldn't tell whether that was the same as the evening working. If closeness could be produced by a procedure, thirty-six items in ascending order of exposure, then what exactly had she learned about Dana, and what had she merely manufactured? Her sister would say she was overthinking it, that the study only opened a door and you still had to walk through it yourself. But her sister hadn't watched Dana answer question twenty-eight, the one about dying, with a specificity that had made the arcade noise seem very far away.

She was still turning it over in the tenth frame, in the honest way that meant she didn't pretend to have settled it, when Dana rolled the last ball of the night and turned around before it reached the pins. "Question thirty-six," Dana said. "Of all the people in your family, whose death would you find most disturbing." Then, after a beat: "You don't have to answer that one. Pick your own. But I get to watch your face while you decide."

The ball hit the pocket and scattered all ten pins, and Megan pulled the folded score sheet out of her back pocket, unwrinkled it, and clicked the pen.

story:
Luca had until Friday to finish the drawing for his application portfolio, and the chair he'd chosen as his subject sat in the reading room of the public library like an accusation. He had picked it because it looked simple: wooden, straight-backed, older than anyone in the building. Three afternoons in a row he had sat cross-legged on the carpet with his sketchbook, and three afternoons the legs had come out wrong, the back slats leaning where they should have stood straight, the whole thing warping on the page like something seen through water. He pressed his pencil down until the lead snapped, then sat very still while the shard rolled off the page onto the carpet.

He had told his mother the portfolio was nearly done. That was the part that sat worst with him, worse even than the drawing. She'd cleared the kitchen table for him and kept his little sister away from his pencils, and every night she asked how it was going, and every night he said good, good, almost there. He knew a word for what he was doing, from a novel he'd read in the fall: mendacity. It had sounded lofty in the novel, almost elegant. In his mouth it just tasted like lying to someone who trusted him.

A girl from his art class, Deja, came through the reading room on Wednesday carrying a stack of returned atlases. She stopped behind him, looked over his shoulder, and said, "That chair looks like it's melting."

"I know." He turned the page sideways, as though the problem might be orientation. It was not orientation.

Deja set the atlases down on the shelf cart and folded herself into the seat across from him. "My grandmother taught me a trick," she said. "You don't draw the chair. You draw what's around the chair. The empty parts. Between the legs, around the back." She tapped the air between two of the chair's legs with one finger, not touching it, like a priest blessing a very small font.

"That makes no sense."

"It's called negative space," she said. "The empty area around and between things. Artists draw that to get the outline right." She picked up his spare pencil, the one he kept behind his ear, and on the corner of his page drew the shapes between the legs: tall thin polygons, a triangle of window light, the wedge of floor shadow. Then she handed the pencil back and went to shelve the atlases, because she was, as she'd told him once, the only sophomore the library would actually pay.

Luca sat for a long moment feeling truculent about it, wanting to tell her that a chair was a chair and you drew a chair by drawing a chair. But the corner of his page sat there with its odd geometry, and the shapes were right. He could see that they were right in a way his chair had never been. The empty parts didn't wobble. They didn't lie.

He started a new page and drew nothing. That was how he thought of it, at first, and it made him laugh under his breath, quietly enough that the man at the microfilm machine didn't glare. He drew the gap between the second and third slat, then the gap between the third and fourth, then the rectangles of window framed by the space around the back, then the air beneath the seat. When he stepped back to the table to look, the chair was there. It had arrived on the page without him drawing it, outlined by its own absence, straight and solid and old. His heart palpitated once, hard, the way it did when a jazz track changed key or when Deja had sat down next to him in September. He looked at the drawing for a full minute before he let himself shade a single plank of the seat.

He was signing his name in the corner, small, when the librarian on desk duty walked over. Mrs. Okafor was heavyset and unhurried and had never once spoken to him except to point at the quiet sign. She looked at the drawing, then at the chair, then back. "You drew the light," she said.

"I drew the gaps," Luca said, which he understood, even as he said it, was the same thing, or near enough, or possibly not the same thing at all, and he decided he could live without deciding.

"Can I put it on the wall by the front?" she asked. "We rotate local student work. It stays yours, you get it back whenever."

He thought of his mother, of telling her tonight that it was done, actually done, done and hanging in a public building. He thought of the strange honesty of the method itself, that you could get at something true by drawing around it rather than at it, and he thought that his whole application essay, maybe his whole next year, might work like that, and then he thought that he might be wrong about all of it, that Friday might come and the portfolio reviewer might want chairs drawn the ordinary way.

"Okay," he said. "Yes."

Mrs. Okafor lifted the sketchbook page with both hands, careful of the corners, and carried it toward the front desk, where the afternoon light came through the tall windows and lay down across the carpet in long, exact shapes.

Kyle had agreed out loud and disagreed quietly, which had lately become his standard arrangement with his father, and which he did not intend to examine too closely.

The new canvas stretched and laced onto the frame well enough, but the painting went wrong almost immediately. He had bought five tubes of paint on impulse at the store, reasoning that more colors meant more choices, and now he sat cross-legged in the grass with them lined up like evidence against him. The blue and the red he had laid down in wide bands curdled against each other, vibrating in a way that made his jaw tighten. It looked petulant, the whole thing, like a tantrum in pigment. He had wanted something steadier for Nadia, something that said he had thought of her, and instead he had produced stripes that fought.

He scraped the worst of it off with a palette knife and went inside to his phone, telling himself he would look for ten minutes. His search for why red and blue hurt each other led him somewhere he did not expect. A physics man, of all people, had something to do with it. Kyle read the page twice, then a third time, because the date seemed too precise to be real.

"Newton," he said aloud to the empty kitchen. "In 1704. In a book called Opticks." He carried the phone back out to the grass and set it face up on the patio stone beside his brushes. Isaac Newton, who had thought about gravity and light, had arranged the colors of the spectrum into a circle, and that circle was an early version of the color wheel artists used today. Kyle sat with that for a while, turning his brushes over. He had assumed the wheel belonged to painters, that some seventeenth-century craftsman had mixed his way to it by feel. Instead a physicist had bent the rainbow into a ring, and painters had inherited the geometry of it.

The wheel told him about opposites. He found a version online, turned it until the red he had used faced its opposite across the circle, and understood that the pair was useful to him for exactly the reason it had wrecked him: the two pushed against each other. So he stopped trying to make the red and blue sit side by side and gave each of them a thin border of the other's opposite, a margin of green around the red, a whisper of orange under the blue, and the bands stopped fighting. They held their ground like neighbors who had finally agreed on a fence.

He worked until the light went long and the sprinklers two yards over came on with their tin hiss. His father came out with a beer and stood at the edge of the patio, saying nothing for the length of a full minute, which Kyle had learned was how the man approached anything handmade.

"Your mother says you learned that circle thing from a scientist," his father said.

"From Newton," Kyle said. "1704. It's in Opticks." He did not add that he had chosen the whole scheme to be calm, or that the calm was for Nadia, or that some part of him had angled the chair on the lawn so it would be visible from the patio. His father drained a third of the beer and looked at the canvas, and the silence stretched, and Kyle noticed that he was holding his breath in a way that had nothing to do with paint.

It was not, he had to admit, a matter of doing it only for himself. He wanted it liked, and he wanted to seem indifferent to whether it was liked, and he could not fully have both. What he could have was the chair, which by dusk was dry enough to touch, its bands lying flat and settled against each other, a consonance he could not have named before this week and which he now saw everywhere he looked: in the fence slats against the grass, in the orange porch light against the coming dark. He folded the chair and carried it toward the garage, and behind him his father said, "Huh," which was not praise and was not nothing, and Kyle kept walking and let it be whichever it was.

story:
Laurence had the ballot spread on the desk beside the keyboard, the paper as long as her forearm, and she was going down the list of judges with three tabs open, because she refused to vote for someone just because their name sounded competent. She was eighteen as of the ninth of this month, which still startled her when she wrote it on forms. Her mother kept passing the doorway with laundry, slowing down each time as if Laurence were performing surgery.

"Grandpa's coming by at four," her mother said on the fourth pass. "He'll want to see that you voted. Try to look excited, or at least awake."

"I'm not excited. I'm reading about a drainage district commissioner." Laurence turned the laptop so her mother could see the candidate's page, a wall of text in a font from another decade. "This guy has been in office since before I was born and his whole statement is two sentences about fiscal responsibility. That's it. That's all he's telling the voters."

Her mother set down the towel she'd been folding. "Then vote for the other one, or don't vote for that one at all. Nobody will arrest you."

"That's not the point." Laurence pulled the laptop back. "If I skip it, I'm letting everyone else decide, and if I vote on nothing, I'm just making noise. I want it to mean something, and I can't tell if it does." She said the last part more quietly than she meant to.

When her grandfather arrived he came in carrying a paper bag of oranges from the tree he babied through every frost, and he put two of them on the desk next to the ballot without comment, which was his way of noticing that she hadn't eaten lunch. He read over her shoulder for a while, hands behind his back, while she clicked between a county measure and an editorial about it.

"Does it matter?" she asked him finally, spinning her chair. "One vote. Everyone says it doesn't."

He picked up an orange and started peeling it in one long spiral, the way he did everything, slowly and without waste. "You know why you get to do this at eighteen?"

"Because of the Constitution. Amendment something."

"Twenty-sixth," he said. "But the push for it had a slogan. Old enough to fight, old enough to vote. Eighteen-year-olds could be drafted for Vietnam, and people said that if you can be drafted, you should get the ballot." He handed her half the orange and sat on the edge of the bed, leaving the rest of it there, not elaborating, which for him was a kind of discipline.

Laurence ate the orange and thought about her grandfather at eighteen, about which of those two things he would rather have been given. She opened a new tab and typed the slogan in, and the results were all there, the marches, the buttons with the words printed in a circle, senators quoted saying exactly that. She read for ten minutes with the peel smell still on her fingers. "So people my age were handed a rifle first," she said, "and the vote was the consolation prize. Or the apology."

"Something like that," her grandfather said. "Depends who you ask."

She looked at the ballot again. The framing helped and it also didn't; the vote wasn't a promise that anything would go her way, and she understood that the slogan was a kind of synecdoche, the draft standing in for every way the country could use you before it let you speak. That didn't make her one ballot weigh more. If anything it made the whole thing feel smaller, a modest, parsimonious little power doled out exactly as far as it had to go and no further, circumscribed on every side by districts and electoral math and commissioners running unopposed since the nineties. And still people had marched for exactly this, this thin slice, because it was what was on offer.

"Okay," she said. She pulled the ballot closer and filled in the drainage race for the challenger, who had at least written a paragraph, and left one judicial race blank where both candidates had given her nothing at all. "I'm not voting in that one. I couldn't tell you why either of them wants the job."

"That's allowed," her grandfather said. "Blank is a answer too."

Her mother appeared in the doorway again, empty-handed this time, and Laurence signed the envelope, licked it, and held the sealed ballot up between two fingers like evidence.

"One vote," she said. "Old enough to fight."

activity: graduating from high school
story:
The march came through the floorboards before Peyton was fully awake, which meant her brother had gotten to the stereo first, which meant today was the day her mother had decided to make ceremonial. She lay in bed and listened to the trumpets loop around the same eight bars, the way they had looped every June of her life, and thought about how strange it was that a person could know a piece of music this well without knowing the first thing about it.

"Band practice at ten," her mother called up the stairs. "And your grandmother's coming to the ceremony, so wear the dress with the buttons."

Peyton had been avoiding the ceremony for weeks, quietly, the way you avoid a thing you can't actually escape. She had tried subterfuge. She had mentioned, at dinner, that plenty of people skipped graduation, that it was long and hot and the speeches were written for parents. She had left a college orientation brochure on the counter with the dates circled, though the orientation wasn't until August. Her mother had absorbed all of it without comment, the way a sea wall absorbs weather, and had gone on ironing.

At ten she was in the band room with her clarinet, running the march for the twelfth time that week, and it was there, counting rests, that the question finally calcified into something she couldn't ignore. "Why this song?" she said, during a water break. "Every school in the country. Every movie. Why do we all play this one?"

"Because it's tradition," said Marcus, who played baritone and considered tradition a sufficient answer to most questions.

"Traditions start somewhere." She was already typing with her thumb, one-handed, the way people did when a question had been sitting in them too long.

What she found was this: the march had become graduation music after it was played at Yale's commencement in 1905, where Edward Elgar received an honorary doctorate of music. She read it twice, then held the phone out so Marcus could see. "Yale. 1905. They gave the composer a doctorate and played his march, and somehow that turned into every cap and gown on earth."

"Creepy," Marcus said, meaning interesting.

"It's not creepy, it's..." She looked for the word and didn't find it. "One school did it once, and now my grandmother is wearing a corsage because of it."

Her grandmother arrived that afternoon, early, while Peyton was still in her robe, and installed herself at the kitchen table with the tea her mother made without being asked. Peyton sat down across from her, mostly because leaving would have required an excuse she didn't have. Her grandmother had grown more ascetic over the years, having given up television, then sugar, then most of her opinions, or at least the sharing of them, so that a visit now felt like sitting with a very calm question.

"I hear you'd rather not walk," her grandmother said.

Peyton examined her tea. "It's a show we put on for other people. I don't need two hours of my name not being called to know I finished."

"You don't," her grandmother agreed, which disarmed her completely. "I skipped mine. 1968. I stood outside in the parking lot in my gown because it was June in Ohio and the gym had no air, and I listened to that same march through the doors." She turned her cup a quarter turn on its saucer. "I remember the music more than I remember deciding anything about it."

Peyton had assumed the argument would be about pride, or photographs, or things her mother could frame. This was something else, and she sat with it while her grandmother drank her tea. There was a version of herself, the one who had tried the brochures and the dinner remarks, that wanted to treat the whole ceremony as an inherited reflex, a thing people did because Yale had done it in 1905 and nobody had thought to stop. But her grandmother standing in an Ohio parking lot in a rented gown, listening through gym doors, was not a reflex. That was a person choosing to be near a thing, even at the edge of it, and Peyton could not make the two ideas sit still together. Maybe the ritual was arbitrary and it meant something anyway. Maybe it meant something because it was arbitrary, because everyone had agreed to it, the way people agreed to a language.

"I'll walk," she said. Her grandmother nodded once, as though Peyton had reported the weather, and asked for more hot water.

At the ceremony the next evening, the band filed in first, and Peyton took her seat in the clarinet section with a good view of the whole procession. When the trumpets came in, she watched her grandmother in the fourth row, leaning slightly forward, doing the same thing she had done in a parking lot in 1968, and Peyton understood that she herself was now part of the reason, the small link that kept the thing running from 1905 to a folding chair in a gym in June. She would not have said that out loud. She wasn't even sure it was true, exactly, and she held onto the uncertainty on purpose, the way she held the clarinet, lightly, at the ready.

She lifted the reed to her lips and came in on the downbeat, half a beat late, and played.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
story:
The letter from the tenant arrived on a Tuesday, and Sebastian's grandfather read it twice at the kitchen table before setting it under the sugar bowl as though to weigh it down. "Mr. Okafor wants his deposit back," he said. "All six hundred of it."

Sebastian had come to the house for the last week of summer, planning mostly to eat his grandmother's cooking and avoid thinking about the fall. Instead he found himself in the passenger seat of the Buick the next morning, riding across town to the little yellow duplex his grandparents had bought decades ago, back when the mortgage on it had seemed to his grandfather like a rope around the neck. "Thirty years we paid," he said at a red light. "Every month. And the bank held the deed until the end, like a hostage." Sebastian had known, in a vague way, that houses were paid for over time, but he had never pictured his grandfather at twenty-five, signing papers at a bank, putting down what he called "the down payment, the part you have to have up front or they won't talk to you at all."

The tenant, Mr. Okafor, met them on the porch. He was maybe thirty, with a moving truck half loaded behind him in the drive, and he wanted, plainly, his money. "I left that place better than I found it," he said. "I painted the kitchen myself. Paid for the paint out of my own pocket."

Inside, the apartment smelled of cardboard and lemon cleaner. Sebastian's grandfather walked the hallway with his hands behind his back, the way he walked his own garden, and stopped at the living room wall where a row of small nail holes marched along the picture rail like a constellation. "There," he said. "Holes in the wall. That's damage. That comes out of the deposit, that's what a deposit is for."

"No," Sebastian said, and both men turned to look at him, and he felt his face go hot, because he had not planned to say anything. But he had spent the previous night at the kitchen table with his grandmother's ancient laptop, wading through an interminable stretch of tenant-rights pages, some written in a lawyerly dialect that assumed an erudition he did not have, until he found one written in plain sentences and read it three times. "The deposit covers unpaid rent or damage beyond normal wear and tear," he said. "Small nail holes are ordinary aging. Where we live, a landlord can't deduct for that."

His grandfather's mouth worked for a moment without sound. "It's my wall," he said finally.

"It's ordinary aging," Sebastian said. "It's on the state website. I took screenshots." He had also done something else, and this was harder to bring up. "Grandpa, I photographed every wall yesterday when we came to measure for the new blinds. Every room, every ceiling corner. Because if Mr. Okafor wants to argue later, you'll want proof of the condition, and so will he."

Mr. Okafor had gone quiet at the mention of the website, and now he cleared his throat. "There's something else," he said. "The back bedroom. There was a leak from the bathroom above it, back in March. I told you about it on the phone." Sebastian's grandfather said that he remembered, and that he had called a plumber. "The plumber patched the pipe," Mr. Okafor said. "The ceiling stain stayed. I didn't cause it, but I didn't fix it either, because it's your building. I figured it would come out of the deposit fight, so I want to say now, before you decide: that stain is mine to live with and yours to fix, and neither of us should pay the other for it."

Here was the twist, and Sebastian watched it happen slowly, like weather changing. His grandfather walked to the back bedroom and stood under the brownish ring on the ceiling for a long time. "That's water damage," he said. "Not from you." He turned around. "I was going to take the six hundred dollars and repaint the whole unit. I had it figured that way. New tenant in September, new paint, and the deposit pays for it."

"Paint wears out," Sebastian said quietly. "Like nail holes."

His grandfather looked at the ceiling, then at the boy, then at the man who had rented his rooms for four years and had never once been late with the rent, and something in his shoulders came down an inch. "The kitchen paint you bought yourself," he said. "What did that cost you?" Mr. Okafor said about eighty dollars. His grandfather took out his checkbook, the old leather kind with a pen loop, and leaned on the windowsill to write. "Six hundred for the deposit," he said, "and eighty for the paint. And you'll indemnify me for nothing, because there's nothing to indemnify. It's just a wall."

Driving home, the windows down, his grandfather was silent for most of the highway. Near the exit he said, "Your grandmother told me you stayed up past one reading that website." Sebastian said that he had. "Good," his grandfather said. "When you get your own place someday, save for the down payment first, then the deposit, and photograph everything, both times, moving in and moving out." He pulled into the driveway and shut off the engine. "Now come inside. She made the plum cake, and she will not cut it without us."

story:
Michael had chosen the cello at the start of term because it looked dignified, but the only instrument left in the storeroom that Friday was a violin with a fine layer of chalk dust along its ribs, so he took it. The music room smelled of rosin and the custodian's lemon floor polish, and the radiators clanked like a stubborn percussion section. Ms. Oyelaran, who ran the after-school ensemble and never wasted words, handed him the bow and said, "Four strings. Everything starts there."

He plucked them that first afternoon, one after another, and they gave back G, D, A, E, lowest to highest, though at the time he only heard four different voices arguing. In the practice rooms along the corridor, other people's scales leaked through the walls, and he wondered whether the intervals between those strings were chosen for a reason, or whether somebody, centuries ago, had simply liked the way they climbed. He had a habit of asking questions like that, and his older sister had once told him he could pontificate about a doorknob. He had looked up the word afterwards, then used it back at her, which she found less amusing than he had hoped.

The ensemble met Tuesdays after last bell, and beside him sat Priya Raman, a tiny pugnacious first-year who had been playing violin since she was six and had opinions about everyone else's posture. Across the stands was Colm, who read music the way other people read street signs, without apparent effort, and who had cornered Michael once at the water fountain to declare that a pianist named Ólafur something-or-other was "the whole zeitgeist now, honestly, the spirit of the age, if you even know what that means." Michael had said he didn't, and Colm had nodded, satisfied, as though this proved something.

The concrete problem arrived in November, three days before the winter showcase, when the second violinist in their quartet broke her wrist on the ice behind the gym. Ms. Oyelaran put a photocopy of the second violin part on Michael's stand and said only, "You know the fingerings. Learn the thinking." Priya leaned over during the break, tapping the four strings with her pencil, one, two, three, four, and recited, like a spell she'd been given long ago by her first teacher: "Good Dogs Always Eat." She pointed from the thickest string upward as she said it. Then she went back to arguing with Colm about tempo, leaving Michael to work out for himself that the letters in her sentence were the names of the strings, that G sat lowest, that E sang highest, and that they were spaced, she mentioned later while packing her case, in perfect fifths, each string to the next.

That night he wrote to his sister at college, because she was the only person he could admit things to. "I got promoted out of desperation, not talent," the letter said. "The second violin part is all inner voices, the plumbing of the piece. Nobody hears you unless you vanish, and then they notice the silence. Also I learned the strings are G, D, A and E, lowest to highest, each a fifth apart, and there's a sentence for it, Good Dogs Always Eat, and I keep saying it in my head like a prayer before every entrance. Is it cheating to use a sentence instead of just knowing? Is that how knowing starts?" He sealed it before he could edit himself into sounding less lost.

The showcase was in the gym, under banners from a fundraiser nobody remembered, and the folding chairs filled with parents holding phones like candles. Colm's opening phrase was clean and a little cold. Priya played with her chin up, daring the audience. Michael came in late on his first entrance, half a beat, and nobody died. On his second entrance he was early, and the chord that resulted was sweeter than the one written, which confused him so much he lost his place for two bars and found it again by feel, by the hum of the G string under his knuckle.

Afterwards, Priya's father took a photograph of the quartet, and Ms. Oyelaran shook each of their hands as though conferring knighthoods. In the coat queue, Priya said, "You dragged on that third phrase. Deliberately?" Michael said maybe, that it had sounded like it wanted to linger, though he couldn't say whether the wanting was his or the music's. Priya considered this the way she considered Colm's tempo arguments, then shrugged and said it had worked. He watched Colm's mother mouth something at Colm across the hall, and Colm, grinning, raised his violin case in answer.

He walked home with the case knocking his hip, saying Good Dogs Always Eat to the frosty street, wondering whether every hard thing began as somebody else's sentence that you slowly earned the right to mean. At his corner he stopped, lifted the case, and unlatched it under the streetlight, just to look at the four strings lying in their perfect ladder. He plucked the E, thin and bright against the cold.

activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Ryan had eleven days to build a portfolio for the state art scholarship, and the Cedar Grove public library was the only place he could print anything larger than his mother's grocery lists. The copier at home choked on cardstock. The school lab charged two dollars a page and closed at four. So on a Tuesday in July he carried his poster design, a protest piece about the river flood two years ago, into the library on a stick drive and asked at the desk about sizes.

The printer offered A3 and A4. He had designed at A4 on his laptop without thinking much about it, because A4 was what the sheets in his backpack were, and A4 was what he could afford. A3 cost more. It also looked more like something a scholarship committee would take seriously, which was a thought he distrusted even as he had it, since it implied the committee would enfranchise whoever spent the most money. His father, who had voted against the levee bond the year before the flood, would have said that judgment was a whole phylum of its own, the kind that sorts people by the price of their paper. His father was not speaking to the county commissioners anymore, though he still spoke to Ryan, mostly about drainage.

The librarian, Mrs. Okonkwo, slid his drive into the machine and printed one A4 and, at Ryan's request, one A3, "just to see." When both sheets came out, Ryan laid them side by side on the table by the window, and something caught at him. He turned the A4 ninety degrees, then back. He put the A4 in the corner of the A3. The corners lined up, both corners, at once.

"Huh," he said.

"Take a pair of scissors to the big one," Mrs. Okonkwo said, not looking up from her returns cart. "Cut it in half, straight across the middle."

He did. He cut the A3 sheet in half and found himself holding two sheets, and when he set one of them over the A4 print, it matched. Not almost, not close enough. Matched, edge to edge, corner to corner, the same shape exactly, his flood poster sitting inside itself with every element landing where it already was.

"The sides are in a ratio of one to the square root of two," Mrs. Okonkwo said, pushing the cart past him toward the stacks. "That's the whole trick. Cut a sheet in half, you get two of the same shape." Then she was gone around the corner, and Ryan stood there with his scissors and his two identical posters feeling like he had been let in on a piece of engineering that had been sitting under his hands his whole life, every notebook and flyer and permission slip he had ever folded in half.

He spent the next hour testing it. He cut the half again, and again, a cascade of shrinking posters marching down the table, the flooded river and the words "WHO DECIDED WHERE THE WATER GOES" reproducing themselves at four sizes, each one true to the last. It was, he thought, a little like the flood itself, the way the water had subdivided the town, alluvial fingers spreading across the low streets, each finger a smaller copy of the breaking. He stopped thinking in that direction because it was the kind of comparison his art teacher called "too neat," and because the poster was supposed to be an argument, not a puzzle.

The argument was the problem. He had made the poster angry. His father's anger, really, borrowed the way he borrowed the truck. And somewhere between the fourth and fifth cut he understood that the same design worked at every size, which meant it worked small, which meant it could be printed cheap, which meant the people the flood had actually damaged, the ones in the rented rooms on Delano Street, could have it too. A poster that only existed at the expensive size was a poster for people who could afford to be angry at a distance. He sat with that for a while, turning the smallest sheet in his fingers.

Then Priya Nair from his calc class appeared at the end of the table with a stack of SAT prep books and an expression of pure, alluvial despair. "Is that the flood thing?" she said. "Oh my god. Cut me one." He cut her one, the quarter size, and she held it up and studied it and said, "You know what's funny, my dad's on the levee commission now, he took the seat after your dad stopped going. He has this exact poster pinned in his garage." She said it kindly, which somehow made it worse and also better, and Ryan laughed, one short surprised bark that got them a look from the front desk.

So the man he had made the poster against had hung it up. Ryan did not know what to do with that and said so, and Priya said, "Maybe he hung it to remind himself who's mad at him," and then went off to find a table near the outlets, taking her quarter-sheet poster with her. He thought about the two ways of reading the same sheet, the way one shape held all its smaller selves, the way his father's anger and the commissioner's guilt might be the same rectangle at different scales, or might not. He couldn't decide, and the scissors couldn't either.

Mrs. Okonkwo came back with the cart and looked at the row of descending posters. "You're paying for that A3," she said.

"I know," Ryan said. He picked up the scissors, cut the smallest sheet in half once more, and put the tiny flood in his shirt pocket.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
story:
The departures board flickered above Gate 14, and Lucas opened his laptop on the seat beside him because the middle seat was empty and might stay that way. His flight to his grandmother's was delayed two hours, which his mother had predicted, and which he had refused to believe until the word DELAYED appeared in amber letters where his departure time used to be. He had a chemistry test to study for and a presentation to finish, and only one of them was due tomorrow, by video, from wherever he happened to be.

The presentation was for his civics class. They were role-playing a town meeting about a proposal to build new housing on a piece of land near the river, and Lucas had been assigned the role of the county's floodplain analyst, which meant he had to sound like somebody who knew things. He did not entirely know things. He had spent three evenings in a geographic information system his teacher had set up, dragging a flood risk layer over a housing layer until the neighborhood he'd grown up in turned blue in some blocks and stayed ordinary gray in others. The overlay was beautiful in a way that unsettled him. His aunt's street was blue.

He had written a draft with the number of houses in the flood zone, forty-one, and he had been almost satisfied with it until he read the assignment sheet again in the airport's harsh light. The mock town council, it said, would ask about residents, not just structures. He stared at the sentence. A council member, playing an obstreperous retired engineer named Mr. Vasquez, was instructed to ask how many people lived in the flood zone, and Lucas's draft answered with houses, which was not the same question and might even be a way of dodging it.

He opened the map and clicked on one blue polygon, a building near the water. A table appeared at the bottom of the screen, and the row that came up had columns: an ID number, a flood classification, a count of residents. He clicked another building and another row rose into the table. So that was how it worked. Each feature in the layer linked to a row in an attribute table, which meant the data attached to buildings, things like the number of residents in each one, could be totaled if he selected an area. He highlighted the whole flood zone, all forty-one polygons, and the table showed him the sum.

Six hundred and twelve people.

He sat with that. Forty-one had felt like a statistic. Six hundred and twelve felt like the gym at his old middle school, which held about that many and looked enormous when it emptied out at the end of an assembly. He texted his aunt, because she actually lived on one of the blue blocks and because she answered faster than anyone he knew.

"Doing my town meeting thing. Did you know there are 612 people in the flood zone by the river?"

Her reply came while the gate agent was announcing something about rebooking. "Who counted us?" she wrote. "Tell whoever it is that the number doesn't include my neighbor's mother, who is in the basement apartment and half the time doesn't answer the door. Also it doesn't include the people who will live in whatever they build. Bring me a coffee when you land."

Lucas read the message twice. She was doing what she always did, taking his clean number and putting a crack in it. The map said six hundred and twelve, and the map was built from data somebody had collected, and data had edges. His aunt's neighbor's mother might be counted or might not. The new residents, if the housing was built, would not be in the table at all yet. He revised his script: he would give the total, and then he would say what the total could not tell them.

He worked until his eyes burned, then bought a sandwich he couldn't really metabolize quickly enough to feel less hungry, and read half a page of enthalpy diagrams for the chemistry test without retaining anything except the shape of the curves. When he boarded at last, the middle seat had been taken by a man who fell asleep before the safety demonstration, and Lucas typed the final lines of his script into his phone with his thumbs.

At the virtual meeting the next afternoon, from his grandmother's kitchen table, Mr. Vasquez performed his role perfectly, arms crossed over a blazer. "Houses, shouses," the boy playing him said. "How many people live in that flood zone, analyst?" Lucas let the pause last one breath, the way he'd practiced.

"Six hundred and twelve," he said. "Each building in the layer links to a row in an attribute table, so I could total the resident counts for the whole selected area. story:
Dominic stood at the counter with his grandfather's Bible open beside a cutting board, the way other people might set a phone next to their dinner. His mother had told him that if he was going to argue with Grandpa Joe about Friday meat, he should at least know what he was arguing from. The lasagna in the oven was the meatless kind, spinach and ricotta, and the smell of it filled the kitchen like an argument already conceded.

"You're doing homework on us now," Grandpa Joe said from the doorway. He set a paper bag on the table. Inside it, Dominic knew, was a pound of ground beef, bought on purpose, a test.

"It's for Mr. Ruiz's class," Dominic said. "We have to debate whether an old religious rule still applies. Using the text itself. Not just feelings about it." He watched his grandfather take down the good knife. "I picked Friday abstinence."

Grandpa Joe began slicing an onion with the patience of a man who had done it fifty years. "You picked a fight, you mean. The McAfees eat burgers on Fridays and sit three pews ahead of us. You want to know if I think they're wrong."

"I want to know why we don't. That's different." Dominic turned the Bible toward him. "The text isn't the problem, Grandpa. It says nothing about beef. It says fasting and abstinence, and it says obey the Church. That's the whole thing."

His grandfather put the knife down. "You finished already? At eighteen?"

Dominic had done research that afternoon, and he was almost afraid to use it. "I found something. Nineteen sixty-six. Pope Paul the Sixth. Paenitemini." He said the word carefully, the way Mr. Ruiz had taught them to say anything in Latin they weren't sure of. "It let the bishops' conferences, the national ones, replace the traditional fast and abstinence with other penance. Prayer. Works of charity. Stuff like that. So it's not that the McAfeys are cheating. It's that somebody changed the rule, and we kept it anyway."

The onion lay in pale rings on the board. Grandpa Joe wiped his hands on the dish towel and did not pick the knife back up. "Who told you that?"

"The Vatican website. Sort of. I had to piece it together." Dominic closed the Bible, then opened it again, because closing it felt like giving up an advantage. "So here's my problem. If the rule can be changed by the same authority that made it, then what makes our way better than theirs? We skip meat. They visit the hospital or whatever. The Church says both count."

"Both count," his grandfather agreed. He sat down at the table across from the beef, which sat there in its wax paper like a third participant. "So go be a McAfee."

The oven timer clicked. Dominic ignored it. "That's not an answer, that's a dare."

"It's an answer. You asked whether the rule still applies. The Church said pray instead, give instead. Fine. So the rule applies, and the shape of it changed." Grandpa Joe folded his arms. "But you want me to say the old shape was nothing. I won't."

Dominic took the lasagna out barehanded, then set it down too fast and sucked his thumb. While he ran it under the cold tap, he thought about Mr. Ruiz's warning that a debater who loved both sides would lose to a debater who loved one. "Here's what I think," he said finally. "The text itself lets the practice change. That's tenable, I can defend it from the documents. But it doesn't say the old practice was wrong, and it doesn't say the new one is equal for every person. Maybe the bishops gave us options because people are different, not because meat was never the point."

"Look at you," his grandfather said, but not unkindly. He stood and got two plates. "Your grandmother used to expatiate on this at dinner. Twenty minutes on sacrifice and hunger, and I'd fall asleep in my chair. You gave me the short version."

"There's a part I can't fix," Dominic said. "For the debate. The other side will ask why we keep the old way when we don't have to. I can say tradition has value. I can say the Friday hunger is a kind of recompense for a week of taking whatever we want. But I can't prove those from the text. They're ours, not its." He served his grandfather the first piece of lasagna. "So I'm going to stand up there and argue the rule still applies, and then admit the part I can't settle. Mr. Ruiz says that costs points."

Grandpa Joe ate one bite, then pushed the plate a few inches away, which for him was an eloquence. He took the pound of beef and put it in the refrigerator, on the bottom shelf, behind the milk where things went to wait for Saturday.

"Put the onion in the fridge," he said. "Half of it's still good."

"You didn't answer about the points."

"Tell your Mr. Ruiz," his grandfather said, "that some questions you lose on purpose."

story:
The licensing office smelled of floor wax and paper, and the number ticket in Anais's hand read 47, which felt like a prophecy of waiting. She had turned eighteen three weeks ago, the last of her friends to do so, and the last to get a learner's permit by an even wider margin. Behind her in line, a boy with a lanyard flapping against his chest kept checking his phone, then checking it again, as though the screen might have changed the posted wait time out of pity.

"Forty-one," the clerk called, and a woman with a toddler on her hip shuffled forward. Anais settled into a plastic chair and read the laminated sign on the wall for the fourth time, mostly because there was nothing else to read. The sign laid out the steps: a learner's permit first, then, after holding it and passing a road test, a provisional license with restrictions, and only then, later, a full license. She had assumed, when she'd imagined this day, that there would be one permit and one test and then freedom. The sign was suggesting something more gradual, an idea she turned over the way she turned over most things her father said too quickly to be examined.

The boy sat down two chairs away. "You here for the road test?" he asked, hopeful, the way people ask in order to be asked back.

"Permit. I'm just starting." She said it plainly, without apology, which surprised her a little.

"Same," he said. "I got mine last month in the next county over. I'm here because we moved." He leaned closer, lowering his voice as if sharing stock tips. "Once I pass the road test next week, my friends and I are driving to the lake. All of us. Someone's got a truck."

Anais glanced back at the sign. "Does the permit thing end when you pass the test?" she asked. "It says here there's a middle step. A provisional license. It has restrictions on it before you get the full one."

He stood up to look, dragging his lanyard along her shoulder in a way that felt accidentally munificent, like being knighted by someone's keys. His face changed while he read. "Restrictions," he said, flatly. He read the line again, mouthing it, as if a second pass might make it say something friendlier. "So I can't just drive my friends around right away."

"Doesn't look like it." She felt the small, mean comfort of knowing something before someone else did, and then felt embarrassed for feeling it, because she had learned it from a sign four minutes ago. She was a neophyte in the exact sense of the word, and the word did not discriminate about how recently the ignorance had been cured.

"That's," he said, and stopped, gesturing at the sign as though it owed him a better verb.

"Forty-seven," the clerk called, and Anais went up to the counter, where a woman with reading glasses on a chain took her paperwork, had her sign a line, and told her to look at a small red dot for the vision check. "Passed," the woman said, with the enthusiasm of a person who said it two hundred times a day, and then: "Instructor's out front, white car. You're her three o'clock."

The white car was parked at the curb with STUDENT DRIVER signs suctioned to both doors, which Anais found both mortifying and weirdly protective, like a sign preempting every possible opinion the surrounding traffic might form about her. The instructor, a small woman named Dot with a clipboard and a thermos, had her adjust the mirror, then the seat, then the mirror again. "Tell me what you see," Dot said, and Anais told her: the curb, a mailbox, a man carrying a birthday cake flat across a parking lot like a pizza.

She pulled out of the space on her second attempt, and the car moved, and it was hers in the way borrowed things can be yours for an hour. At the first stop sign she braked too hard and both of them rocked forward. "Gentle," Dot said, sipping from the thermos without apparent concern for her own life. "You have time. Everything today is gradual." Anais laughed, surprising herself, because that was the second time today someone had told her that, and she was beginning to think the licensing office knew something the rest of the world was too polite to say. When they turned back toward the lot, the boy with the lanyard was standing at the curb, phone at his ear, holding up a hand as if to wave or to ask a question.

Anais rolled down the window, and he leaned in and said, "So how bad is it, out there?"

story:
The clock above the whiteboard read 10:47, and Ava had promised herself she would not look at her phone until lunch. Mr. Ferris had left the classroom for the copy room, which meant thirty-two minutes of unsupervised study hall, which meant her application status sat one login away in her pocket like a stone. Around her, the AP Gov class she was technically auditing argued about a populist senator from Ohio, someone who had apparently promised to defund the very agency he'd once run. Her friend Deshawn kept calling him a genius of resentment. Her notebook was open to a page that said, in her own handwriting, nothing about any of it.

What it said instead was a list she'd made at two in the morning: reasons Wellesley, reasons State. Under reasons Wellesley she'd written small classes, the lake, the tour guide with the clogs. Under reasons State she'd written money, and then, because she was honest even at two in the morning, near Mom.

The tour had been in October. She and her mother had flown east on miles her mother had saved from work trips, and on the second morning a senior in clogs had walked them backward along a brick path, narrating the buildings like a person who had memorized a poem. At the admissions office she stopped and gestured at the glass doors as if presenting a cathedral. "Our yield this year was the highest in a decade," she said, and half the parents nodded as though they knew what that meant.

Ava hadn't known. She'd raised her hand, feeling like the only person in the group willing to be the ignorant one. "What's yield?"

The guide had smiled, the practiced smile of someone who got this question twice a day. "Yield is the percentage of students a college admits who actually accept the offer and enroll."

That was all she'd said, but Ava had turned it over the whole flight home. A college admitted a hundred people and only some came. The college was guessing, the same way she was guessing, and its prestige depended on being guessed right. Her mother, watching the clouds, had offered something jaundiced about how the whole thing was a beauty contest where everyone pretended not to care who won. Ava had argued with her then. She was less sure now, three days after the email that said her file had been deferred to regular decision, which was the admissions office's way of saying maybe without saying it.

Now the clock said 10:52. Deshawn leaned across the aisle. "You're going to wear a hole in that page. Just check it."

"My brother absconded with my charger, my phone's at nine percent, and if it dies mid-decision I'll lose my mind."

"Then wait for a plug."

"Then wait forever." She said it lightly, but the truth underneath it was heavier: part of her preferred the waiting, because the waiting had two doors in it. In April, or whenever the letter came, there would be only one. She had been turning that over too, the strange double vision of it. From the outside she was a supplicant, a percentage point the college would either claim or not. From the inside she was the one choosing, with a list on one page and a mother on the other, and the college's yield was made of nothing except thousands of girls exactly like her deciding. Both things were true at once, and she couldn't make them into one thing, and she was starting to think she wasn't supposed to.

Mr. Ferris came back with his copies, and the argument about Ohio resumed, and at 10:58 Ava gave up and slid the phone out under the desk. The login screen loaded slowly, the way screens do when they know. She typed her password wrong once, then right. The wheel spun. Deshawn had stopped pretending to read.

The page resolved. There was a block of text, and at the top of it, before she could read a single word, one line stood out in bold: Congratulations on your admission.

Her thumb hovered over the screen. Somewhere in Ohio a senator was promising things, and somewhere on a brick path a girl in clogs was still walking backward, and Ava had until May 1 to decide. She looked up at Deshawn.

"Get me a charger," she said. "I have to call my mom."

story:
Angelina arrived eleven minutes early, which she decided was the correct amount of early: enough to claim the good table by the window, not so much that she looked desperate. She ordered a cappuccino she didn't especially want, because holding a warm cup gave her hands something official to do, and spread a paperback across the table's second chair so no one else would take it. The book was her roommate's, a fat psych text she'd grabbed on the way out the door for exactly this purpose, a prop, a shield.

The date was with Theo, whom she'd met at orientation where he'd spent forty minutes defending the campus poetry slam to a table of skeptics, not preaching so much as proselytizing, though he did it with such goofy charm that even the skeptics had softened. When he walked into the coffee shop he was carrying a paper bag that leaked the smell of cinnamon, and he held it up like evidence. "I didn't know what you'd want," he said, "so I got three kinds of pastry. This is either thoughtful or alarming."

"It's both," Angelina said, and moved the book so he could sit.

They talked the way people talk when everything about a person is still unverified. He told her about his brother, who worked at a shelter downtown and came home every night furious and energized, impossible to talk to about anything except the residents, the indigent men who'd become, in his brother's telling, more real to him than his own family. She told him about her mother's restaurant, the year it nearly closed, the regulars who'd quietly paid for other people's meals. He listened with his whole face. She kept noticing that she was noticing it.

Then, because the universe apparently had a sense of humor about first dates, the espresso machine behind the counter died with a sound like a car backfiring, loudly, inches from Angelina's shoulder. She startled so hard she knocked the cappuccino into her lap. The barista, a broad-shouldered woman named Kim according to her nametag, vaulted the counter with a towel before Angelina had finished gasping, pressing it against the spill on the table and then, more gently, offering a second one for Angelina's jeans. "You okay? That thing's been threatening to blow for a week." Theo had jumped too, his chair legs shrieking against the floor, and now they were both standing, both shaky, both laughing at nothing in particular.

They sat back down, and Angelina found that her heart was pounding, hard, and that she felt strangely, vividly alive, the way the room looked after lightning: every edge sharper. She looked at Theo, at the concern still crinkled around his eyes, at the pastry bag he'd half-risen to protect, and something in her chest performed a small, definite flip, and she thought, with the certainty of a person who has just been frightened within an inch of her life: I really like him.

For a while she rode that feeling. He refilled her water without being asked; she caught herself smiling at the ice in the glass. But a doubt began to gnaw at her, because she'd been ambivalent about this date all week, and ambivalence doesn't usually dissolve in one loud noise. She turned her phone over and over on the table. Finally, feeling like a fraud, she opened a text to her roommate and typed: how do you know if you like someone or if you're just scared of espresso machines.

The reply took a minute. Then: omg open the book. Ch 11. She was still under the table fishing for the textbook when Theo asked what she was doing, and she decided, on impulse, to be honest, or at least honest-adjacent. "My roommate told me something's in here that I need to read. It's about tonight, possibly. It's very embarrassing." She found the chapter, thumbed through it, and read faster than she'd ever read anything, her cheeks heating while Theo watched with open fascination.

"Okay," she said, setting the book down flat between their cups. "So there's this thing. Psychologists call it misattribution of arousal. A racing heart caused by fear or excitement gets mistaken for attraction to the person nearby."

Theo blinked. "So the espresso machine."

"So the espresso machine." She pulled the book back before he could read over her shoulder, because the margins were now mortifyingly relevant. "The problem is that knowing about it doesn't turn it off. My heart doesn't know it's been caught. So I can't tell which part of what I'm feeling is you and which part is a broken machine, and I might not be able to tell for a while. Possibly ever. I just didn't want to sit here pretending I was sure when I wasn't."

He tore the bag open between them, releasing cinnamon into the air, and set the largest pastry on her napkin. "Then we'll have to do it again," he said. "Somewhere with no machinery. A field, maybe." Angelina laughed, and noticed, carefully, the way her heartbeat answered, and left it there, unresolved, still pounding, while she reached for the pastry and broke it in half.

story:
The last box in Victor's room was labeled MISC, which was a lie, because he knew exactly what was in it: the folded map of Cedar Run with everyone's houses marked in pen, a stripped bike chain, half a deck of cards, and a photo from junior year that he kept face down at the bottom so his mother wouldn't ask about it. The truck came at seven in the morning. That gave him one evening, and Marcus had already texted three times asking whether he was coming to the quarry or whether he was going to be a ghost about it.

He went. The water was still cold for May, and they jumped off the low ledge because the high one belonged to a summer they weren't going to share. Marcus tried to excoriate him on the walk back, saying Victor had gotten quiet weeks ago, that he'd started leaving early, that a person could at least pretend he was being torn apart. Victor let him run out of words, because most of it was true, and because the alternative was saying what he actually suspected: that leaving might not tear him apart, and that felt worse.

At dinner his sister Priya, home from her first year of college, was scrolling through her psych notes with her laptop propped against the ketchup. "Help me study," she said, shoving it across. "Flashcards. I'll test you." He was in no mood, but the alternative was taping boxes, so he read while she ate.

One card stopped him. Robert Zajonc, 1968, experiments on what the card called the mere-exposure effect: people tend to like things more simply because they have seen them more often. He read it twice. Priya, chewing, said, "Mere-exposure effect. It's on the exam." He set the card down like it was warm.

"Say the answer anyway," she said.

"People tend to like things more simply because they've seen them more often. Zajonc, 1968."

"Good. Next."

But he wasn't hungry anymore, and he wasn't exactly upset. He was working something out, sitting there with his fork down. He thought about how, in fourth grade, he'd hated the smell of the cafeteria until he didn't. He thought about Marcus himself, whom he'd disliked for the first month of seventh grade, before their lockers happened to be adjacent and the dislike quietly expired. He thought about Priya's roommate, who had hated her bus route in a new town and found it almost comforting a month later, a story Priya told every Thanksgiving that he had never once believed until now.

"What if that's the whole thing," he said. "Not just bus routes. What if I'm not even going to miss this place the way I think I will. What if it's just exposure, and the new town becomes the familiar thing, and Cedar Run becomes the strange one, and I don't get a say in any of it."

Priya closed the laptop halfway. "That's not what the card says. The card says you'll like the new stuff more than you expect. It doesn't say you'll like the old stuff less." She looked at him the way she did when she was deciding whether he could take the truth. "You could take the card as mercy. Or you could take it as an insult to everyone you love. It's not deciding for you."

He didn't answer, because he had asked himself the same question in the shower for two weeks and never gotten further than the question. Whether Marcus was a person or a habit. Whether either of them would still recognize the difference by Christmas.

At ten he drove to Marcus's house, which was against the plan, because the plan had been the quarry and then goodbye, and plans had a way of becoming the shape of a thing if you let them. Marcus was on the porch. The porch light was on and moths worked at it, and the map was folded in Victor's back pocket.

"Come see something," Victor said, and spread the map on the porch boards and took out the pen. He drew the route to the new town, the highway, the exit his father had already driven twice. Then he marked the new house with a small square, the way their own houses were marked. "This is going to be a real place," he said. "I'm going to see it every day. And apparently that's how liking starts, whether or not I want it to." Marcus looked at the map, then at him, and Victor said, "It might happen to you too. This place without me in it. It's not a decision anyone makes."

Marcus picked up the pen, turned it once in his fingers, and drew a line from his own marked house straight to the new square, longer than any line on the map, crossing three towns and a river that the highway didn't even cross. Then he wrote along it, in small letters, exposure.

They sat with the porch light on until Victor's phone buzzed with his mother's curfew, and the moths kept circling, faithful to the one bright thing they knew.

story:
The week before Noah left for college, his father handed him a shovel and pointed at the fence line where the last strip of switchgrass separated their bean field from the Halversons' plowed ground. "Pull it out if you want," his father said, "or leave it. It's yours next summer either way." Four acres of grass, four acres that could have been beans at fourteen dollars a bushel, standing there like a spare tire nobody needed. Noah had spent all of July building the case against it, rehearsing numbers in his head the way his debate coach had taught him, but he hadn't said any of it aloud yet.

Then the orientation schedule arrived, and his first Friday of classes included a field trip to the Okafor farm, forty minutes south of campus, for everyone in the agricultural systems survey course. Noah almost skipped it. He had grown up on a farm; he knew more about dirt than the professor did, probably. But attendance was ten percent of the grade, so he boarded the bus with his earbuds in and his arms crossed, watching the tile lines scroll past the windows.

Mrs. Okafor met them at the gate in a canvas jacket, the wind pulling at her collar. She was younger than Noah expected, and she didn't lecture. She just started walking the boundary of her west field, and the class trailed after her through stubble and loose chaff, and when the wind gusted she stopped and let them all feel it, grit ticking against their jacket zippers like sleet. "Notice where it stings and where it doesn't," she said, and kept walking.

The field was striped. Bands of corn ran between bands of tall grass, maybe twenty rows of each, all the way to the creek. A girl from Chicago asked why the farm looked like that, like a barber pole, and Mrs. Okafor squatted down and pulled up a fistful of grass, roots dangling a foot and more below it, pale and matted and heavy with soil. "In the Dust Bowl, the Plains' native grasses got plowed up, and with them the deep roots that held the soil. Then the drought came and the wind carried the topsoil away." She let the root mass dangle a moment longer, then set it back in the ground and tamped it with her boot, as if returning a borrowed thing.

Noah stood at the back of the group and felt his argument rearranging itself under him. He had been thinking about the grass strips as sentiment, his grandfather's habit dressed up as virtue, something you paid for out of nostalgia. He hadn't thought of them as machinery. The wind was still coming off the Halversons' side of the fence line even here, forty minutes from home, and it stung on the bare patches and went quiet in the grass, exactly as she'd said it would.

On the bus back he called his father. "I'm not pulling the switchgrass out," he said. His father said nothing for a while, long enough that Noah could hear the radio in the kitchen, the grain report, noxious weed notices for two counties over. "You had that whole speech ready," his father said finally. "I could hear you practicing it through the screen door. Fourteen dollars a bushel. I know the number." Noah looked out the window at a tractor turning on a far field, its dust plume rising and leaning east. "The grass is holding the field down," Noah said. "That's income too. It's just income you can't see until the year you'd lose everything else."

There was a silence on the line that Noah couldn't read, and he was honest enough with himself to admit it. Maybe his father was proud. Maybe he was recalculating the farm's whole ledger. Maybe he was just tired and had stopped listening. Noah's roommate, a business major who heard only the word income, leaned over from the next seat and said, "So did you convince him, or did he convince you?" and Noah said, "Neither, I think. I changed my own mind with somebody else's information," which sounded clumsy out loud, and which his roommate repeated in a mock-elocution voice, hand to his chest, until the girl from Chicago told them both to shut up.

That Sunday, the wind came up hard out of the northwest, thirty miles an hour and rising, and Noah drove home to walk the fence line before he left for good. The Halversons' field, disked bare for winter wheat, had already begun to travel; a brown haze hung over the low ground, and the ditch on their side of the fence had a new shoulder of fine soil drifted against the wire, soft as ash. On his family's side, the bean stubble was brown and ugly but fixed, and the switchgrass ran down the slope in a gold line, hissing, its seed heads bent all one direction, and along its upper edge the drifted soil had piled six inches deep, held there, bought and paid for in a currency no market quoted.

His father came down the fence line to meet him, hands in his pockets, and stood looking at the drift. "Halverson called this morning," he said. "He wants to know if we've still got seed for that grass." Then he laughed once, short, almost regretful. "Forty years I've been telling your grandfather those strips were wasted ground. Now the man who out-yielded me every season of my life wants my weeds." He bent and picked up a handful of the drifted topsoil, let the wind burnish it off his palm grain by grain, and said, "Go get the seed catalog out of the truck."
