Edouard set the lasagna down between his mother's geraniums and his brother's phone, and immediately his father began. "So the hero of the hardware store returns. Tell them what you did."

The facts were simple enough to say out loud, though they had been undulating in Edouard's head all afternoon like something alive in a jar. On Tuesday he had suggested to Mr. Kastner, the owner, that the store stay open an hour later on weekdays. More contractors would come after their jobs ended; the numbers Edouard had pulled from the register tapes supported it. Mr. Kastner had clapped him on the shoulder and said he'd think like an owner someday. Then, on Thursday, the new schedule went up, and the closing shift started at six, which was exactly when the last bus to Cedar Heights left the depot. Rosa, who had worked closings for nine years, lived in Cedar Heights. So did Marcus and the two college kids hired in May.

"Edouard," his mother said. "Your father is being facetious. Eat."

"I'm being serious. This is a serious dinner." His father forked a piece of garlic bread and pointed it like a citation. "My son improves the store's revenue and strands three employees at the curb. That's a trade-off, that's what that is. You learn about those in your ethics class? They have a name for everything now."

"They have a name for this one, actually." Edouard had spent his lunch period in the library with his phone face down on the table, searching until he found it. "There's a professor, Freeman, wrote a book in 1984, Strategic Management: A Stakeholder Approach. He argued that a business should consider everyone affected by its decisions, not only the owners. Anyone affected counts as a stakeholder. Customers, workers, the neighborhood." Saying it aloud at the table felt strange, like reciting something in a language he was not yet fluent in.

His brother, Timmy, looked up from his phone long enough to say, "So the bus people are stakeholders and Dad's a stakeholder and the store's a stakeholder. Everybody's a stakeholder. Great system, very rigorous."

"Everyone affected," Edouard said. "That's the point. That's the whole point, actually." He was surprised by how steady his voice came out, because inside he was not steady at all. He had made a recommendation with a spreadsheet and a guess about traffic, and the spreadsheet had been right, and the guess had been right, and Rosa had still ended up standing on Delaware Avenue at six-fifteen yesterday, waiting for a ride that came forty minutes late. He'd seen her from the bus window on his way home. He had almost gotten off. He had stayed in his seat, which was its own decision, and he could not stop weighing it.

"Did you say anything to Kastner?" his mother asked. She had stopped eating, which in her case was the equivalent of standing up and shouting.

"I went back this morning before school. I told him about the bus." Edouard pushed the lasagna around his plate, red sauce pooling in the trench his fork made. "He said he'd look at carpooling options. He said, and this is a quote, 'Good catch, that's why I pay you to think.' Except he doesn't pay me to think about that part. He pays me to think about the register. I thought about the register and something else happened, something I wasn't looking at."

"Unintended consequences," his father said, with the grim satisfaction of a man who had predicted rain all day and was now watching it pour. "You didn't intend to strand Rosa. Intentions don't carry people home, though."

"Right, but here's what I keep going back and forth on." Edouard put his fork down, which his family all noticed, because he never put his fork down. "If I'd thought about everyone affected, if I'd actually applied the thing instead of just finding it Thursday night like a lawyer hunting for a precedent to excuse himself with, would I have made a different recommendation? Maybe. Maybe I'd have said close at five-thirty and open earlier. Or maybe I'd have said the same thing, because the store is struggling, because Mr. Kastner has three kids in college, because he's a stakeholder too, and the whole thing is a trade-off between people who all have real claims. The book gives you the question. It doesn't do the arithmetic for you."

Timmy lowered the phone entirely, which had not happened at a dinner table since March. "So what are you going to do?"

"Monday I'm going to ask Mr. Kastner for the schedule through August, before it's posted, not after. Not to reverse anything. Just to look at all of it at once, bus times and register tapes together, and see what's actually possible." He picked the fork back up. "Maybe nothing changes. Maybe the honest answer is that the extra hour pays for a shuttle van. I don't know yet. I'm telling you I don't know yet, and I'd rather say that than pretend I solved it in the library at lunch."

His mother spooned more lasagna onto his plate without asking, which was how she said she was listening. His father opened his mouth, closed it, and ate the garlic bread instead. Through the window the geraniums moved in the evening wind, and Timmy said, "Stakeholder theory at the dinner table. Verisimilitude achieved. This family finally resembles an actual household."

"Shut up and pass the bread," Edouard said, and passed it to Rosa in his head, forty minutes late, still waiting under the streetlight.

story:
The cake had his name on it in blue icing, which Brayden took as a small omen, since blue was the color of the college logo on the banner his mother had taped above the buffet. He had not yet told anyone that he was thinking of deferring a year, and the banner seemed to presage the conversation he would have to have before the ice cream melted. He stood near the deviled eggs and practiced openings in his head.

His grandfather arrived late, as always, holding a folded newspaper under one arm like a man reporting for duty. He shook Brayden's hand formally, then ruined it by pulling him into a hug that smelled like spearmint and engine grease. "Eighteen," he said. "Legal adult. You can now be sued."

"I'll try to avoid insolvency," Brayden said, mostly to make his cousins laugh, and they did, except for the youngest, who asked what insolvency meant and was told to eat his potato salad.

Dinner was long and loud. An uncle who had once declared bankruptcy, a fact the family handled the way it handled weather, held forth on the stock market with a jaundiced eye, and Brayden's mother kept refilling glasses as though hydration were the family's only remaining defense. When the toasts began, his grandfather stood, tapped his glass, and did not say what everyone expected.

"I never graduated," he said. "High school, I mean. I left in eleventh grade."

The room recalibrated. His mother set down a pitcher. Someone's fork stopped halfway.

"I went in the Army instead," his grandfather continued, apparently addressing the potato salad. "And afterward, I got the GED. That test they made in 1942, so service members and veterans who hadn't finished high school could show they had the skills anyway. That was me. I took it after I got out."

"The same year," Brayden's aunt said, "as the Chopin concert?"

"The same lifetime," his grandfather said, and sat down, having concluded his remarks.

Later, Brayden found him on the porch with a slice of cake he wasn't eating, the fork laid across the plate at a precise angle. The yard was turning the color of late evening, and somewhere a sprinkler ticked against a fence.

"You never told me that," Brayden said.

"Never came up."

"I've known you eighteen years."

"Seventeen and some months. You weren't conversational at first."

Brayden sat on the step below him. In the window behind them, his mother was cutting more cake for cousins who hadn't finished their first pieces, an act of optimism the family had long since learned not to question. He had been rehearsing a speech all week about the gap year, the job at the machine shop, the idea that a diploma was a door and not a floor, and now every version of it sounded different in his head.

"I've been thinking about not going," he said. "In the fall. Right away, I mean. Working first."

His grandfather didn't answer right away. He picked up the fork, then set it down again, and Brayden understood that this was the older man thinking, not dismissing.

"You know what I used to think the GED was?" his grandfather said. "Secondhand. A substitute thing. Took me years to notice nobody who mattered ever asked which one I had. Then I trained fellows who had the regular diploma and couldn't read a schematic, and I stopped sorting people that way, including myself." He looked at the yard. "On the other hand, the Army didn't give me a choice about waiting. You have one. That's not nothing either."

"So which is it?"

"If I knew that, I'd have written a book instead of engines." He handed the plate down. "Take this in, would you. Your mother's giving me the look."

Brayden carried the cake through the sliding door, past the banner, past the uncle now explaining interest rates to a teenager who was texting under the table. His mother met his eyes across the room with a question in them, and he realized he still didn't have the answer, only something closer to it, and that his grandfather had left both pieces of it on the porch, next to a fork nobody had used.

He set the plate on the buffet, and before he could turn around, his mother said, "Brayden. Come here a second."

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
story:
Anthony got to statistics early because the only seat near the window was in the back, and he liked watching the parking lot fill. Mr. Ruiz had written a number on the board before anyone arrived, 48 to 46, and beneath it the words "City Council Poll, Channel 5." When the bell finished, Dana Vasquez stood up before Mr. Ruiz could say anything.

"Can I present?" she asked. She had been trying for two weeks to get the school to fund a student survey project, and Mr. Ruiz had told her she could have five minutes of class if she brought data. She walked to the board with her laptop and clicked to a slide with a bar chart. "I put a poll on the school's app asking whether we should keep open lunch or go to closed blocks. I got 1,400 responses. Nine percent more said open. So the student body wants open lunch, and I want the administration to actually look at it at the next board meeting." Her voice was steady, but her thumbnail was pressed white against the clicker.

Anthony liked Dana, and he wanted open lunch too, but something about the slide bothered him, the way the bars were drawn tall and certain. He raised his hand. "Who answered?"

"People who use the app."

"Who uses the app?"

"Mostly freshmen," she admitted. "Because the freshmen got the orientation push."

Marcus, two rows over, leaned back in his chair. "It's 1,400 people, man. Out of like 2,000 in the school. That's basically everybody. If that many people say it, it's right." A few people nodded. Marcus wanted the argument settled quickly; he had a calculus test next period and no patience for a debate that would eat the review time.

Anthony didn't have an answer ready, so he said the only true thing he had. "Big doesn't automatically mean right." It sounded weak even to him, a slogan without a body. Mr. Ruiz, who was leaning against the radiator with his arms folded, said nothing, which Anthony had learned meant the teacher thought the question was live.

At lunch Anthony went to the library and typed "famous wrong polls" into a search, half expecting nothing, and the screen filled with the same story three times. In 1936 a magazine called the Literary Digest mailed out a survey about the presidential election and collected about 2.4 million responses, and on the strength of those numbers predicted that Alf Landon would beat Franklin Roosevelt. Roosevelt then won in a landslide. Anthony read it twice. He wrote nothing down and then wrote it down anyway, the number and both names, because 2.4 million felt impossible to hold in his head. Whatever it was that made a poll wrong, it wasn't a shortage of people. Something else decided.

He found Dana in the hallway before seventh period, by the water fountain where the noise covered conversation. "That thing you said about 1,400 being basically everybody. There was this poll in 1936, the Literary Digest. They got 2.4 million responses and said Landon would beat Roosevelt, and Roosevelt won in a landslide."

Dana looked at the number on his notebook. "2.4 million."

"Yeah."

"So what was wrong with it?"

"I don't know yet. I'm working on that part." He could have guessed, something about who ended up in the sample and who didn't, freshmen and app users and magazine readers in 1936, but he didn't want to dress a guess up as knowledge. What he did know was the shape of it: the size of a sample and the truth of a claim were different axes, and the first did not guarantee the second. He told her that much, and she chewed her lip, and he could see her weighing her board meeting against it.

That night they sat in his kitchen with the textbook open to the chapter they hadn't reached yet, the one on sampling distributions. There was a formula for how far off a percentage could plausibly be, called the margin of error, and it shrank as the sample grew, but slowly, like a door closing by degrees. They ran Dana's numbers. With 1,400 responses her 9 percent lead survived, comfortable even. Then she pulled up the breakdown by grade and the floor dropped out of the argument: seniors were nearly absent from her data, and seniors were the ones who remembered the closed-block year. Whether the whole school preferred open lunch depended on people who hadn't answered, and no amount of arithmetic could allay that doubt. It wasn't happenstance that her sample skewed young, either; the orientation push had built the skew in, quietly, a subterranean bias under an impressive-looking total.

"So I can't take it to the board like this," Dana said. She said it flatly, and then, after a minute, "Unless I take it like this. Nine percent overall, but the sample is mostly underclassmen, and I need two hundred more seniors before the number means anything."

"That's more honest than the slide was."

"It's less persuasive."

"It might be more," Anthony said. "They're the ones who always say student government fakes its data."

They stayed at the table past ten, drafting the email she would send out, deciding to go classroom to classroom in the senior wing on Thursday instead of relying on the app. Dana typed the subject line, erased it, and typed it again. "Seniors," she read aloud, "we want your answer, even the ones of you who never check anything."

"Especially those," Anthony said, and reached over her shoulder to hit send.

activity: going on a first date
story:
Henry arrived at the Beanery eleven minutes early, which he told himself was a matter of the bus schedule and nothing else, and which was, in fact, a matter of wanting to choose the table near the window before Marisol got there so that he would appear to have been there for ages, casual, at home. He set down his backpack, took out his history notes on the Mongol expansion across the steppe for Tuesday's quiz, and then put them away again because studying on a date, even before the date technically began, seemed like something a person would do to seem interesting rather than something an interesting person would do.

Marisol came in at 4:02, shaking rain off her jacket, and Henry stood up so fast he knocked his spoon to the floor. He had liked her since the group project in October, when she had eviscerated his draft thesis in one sentence and then spent forty minutes helping him rebuild it, and he had decided, over three months of deliberation, that this was a good sign and not a warning. He got in line with her, bought her drink even though she protested, and carried both cups back to the window table with the concentration of a bomb technician.

They were eight minutes into a genuinely decent conversation about whether the school's new bell schedule was gratuitous cruelty or merely incompetence when Priya walked in with Dylan. Priya was Henry's best friend since sixth grade; Dylan was two years older, had a car, and had been dating her for five weeks. Henry watched them order, and he watched Dylan take Priya's wrist to steer her toward a table, and he watched Priya's face do something brief and small that she smoothed over immediately. Henry noticed all of this and told himself he noticed it because Dylan was, objectively, a jerk, and not for any other reason, and certainly not because Priya had once, in eighth grade, held his hand during the whole of a thunderstorm and neither of them had ever mentioned it since.

He kept half his attention on their table while Marisol described her brother's wedding disaster. Dylan reached across and gripped Priya's forearm when she reached for her phone, hard enough that she set the phone down and laughed, a laugh with no floor under it. Twice. Three times, over twenty minutes. Henry was not counting, except that he was.

"Sorry," he said to Marisol. "My friend's over there. Her boyfriend keeps grabbing her arm and it doesn't look like a joke kind of grabbing."

Marisol glanced over, unhurried. "That's the third time."

"You were counting too?"

"Hard not to." She wrapped both hands around her cup. "Is she the type to say something if you ask?"

Priya was the type to eviscerate anyone who suggested she couldn't handle her own life. That was the problem. Henry had a page torn from a health class handout folded in the front pocket of his backpack, something he'd shoved there in September and rediscovered last week while looking for a pencil: the CDC's 2021 Youth Risk Behavior Survey, which had found that about one in twelve US high school students who had dated reported experiencing physical dating violence. One in twelve. He had read it twice on the bus, wondering which twelve-person rows of his classes it applied to, and whether the numbers counted only the people who reported it, and what the unreported rows would look like. He had not thought, at the time, that he might someday watch it happen from four tables away.

"I read this thing," he said now, quietly, because Marisol was watching him and he did not want Priya to hear. "A CDC survey, 2021, the Youth Risk Behavior Survey. About one in twelve high school students who'd dated reported physical dating violence." He heard how it sounded, like a lecture, like a trivia card. "I'm not saying that's her. I'm saying it's common enough that it's not crazy to say something."

"It's not crazy," Marisol said.

"It might be me being a bad friend instead. Or a jealous one." He said it before he could stop himself, and it sat on the table between them alongside the two cups. Marisol didn't reach for it or brush it away, which he appreciated more than he could have said.

He got up, crossed the four tables, and stood beside Priya's chair with his hands in his pockets. "Hey. Can I borrow you for a sec? Help me pick a drink for Marisol."

Priya followed him to the counter, and Dylan watched them go with an expression Henry decided not to interpret. At the counter Henry looked at the menu board as though it required study, and then at her forearm, where the marks were already fading.

"Dylan grabs you," he said. "Your arm. I've seen it three times tonight and you don't look like you like it."

Priya stared at the pastries case. "It's not a thing."

"If it's not a thing, then it's not a thing to talk about either. So talk about it."

"It's a thing," she said finally, very quietly, to the glass.

"Okay," Henry said. "Then you don't have to figure it out standing at this counter tonight." He nodded toward the window table, where Marisol had turned her chair to give them privacy, or the appearance of it. "Come sit with us. Bring your coffee."

Priya glanced back at Dylan, then at the door, then at the window.

"Okay," she said.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
story:
Olivier had folded the population pyramid of Japan into his jacket pocket before leaving the house, and by the second switchback of the trail it had gone soft with sweat, so that when he pulled it out at the overlook it opened like something alive. His uncle's dog, a gray-muzzled thing called Pim, sat down beside him and watched the paper as though it might bolt. The graph was for his first college assignment, due in nine days, though the professor had said the deadline was the least interesting part of it. On the left of the pyramid the bars ran long and fat near the middle, like a barrel cinched at both ends. On the right, near the top, the bars flared out wider than their neighbors on the left, and Olivier had been staring at that asymmetry for two days without making sense of it.

He had tried asking his younger sister, Marta, who was good at guessing. "Maybe they counted wrong," she'd said at breakfast, chin in her hand. "Or maybe more men leave the country." Then she had leaned closer, tapped the widest bar at the very top of the right side, and said, "Or maybe women just live longer than men, and that's all it is." She'd shrugged and gone back to her toast, leaving Olivier with the strange feeling of having been handed an answer that was either obvious or wrong, with no way to tell which.

The trail continued up through pines, and he kept walking with the paper refolded, Pim trotting ahead. The assignment wanted a prediction: from the pyramid alone, would the country need more schools or more nursing homes in thirty years. The professor had warned them against what she called charlatan confidence, people who read one demographic shape and pronounced the future like oracles. Olivier liked that warning. It made the work feel less like arithmetic and more like judgment, though he wasn't yet sure what judgment consisted of besides noticing things slowly.

He noticed, first, the base of the pyramid: narrow. Fewer children being born than there were people in the middle ages, which meant the middle would thin over time, and the whole shape would drift upward like oil in water. More schools or more nursing homes. The question had seemed almost insulting in its simplicity until he understood that the answer was both, in different decades, and that the pyramid could tell you the order. A country could need classrooms now and wards later, and the graph held that sequence in its silhouette the way a tree ring held a drought.

What he couldn't reconcile was the tilted top. If Marta was right, if women lived longer than men on average, then the right side of the pyramid, which was the female side, would naturally widen at the top, and the widening told you nothing about births or policy; it was, he thought, extrinsic to the question, a feature of the shape that came from longevity rather than from any decision the country had made. But then he stopped himself on the trail, because was that true? A nursing home population was mostly women if women mostly lived to fill it. The asymmetry wasn't beside the point. It changed who the nursing homes were for.

He sat on a granite slab near the third overlook and ate half a sandwich while Pim investigated a chipmunk hole with professional seriousness. His professor had said something in the first lecture about learning to historicize a statistic, to ask when and where it was true before trusting it, and Olivier had written the word down without feeling it. Now he felt it. The pyramid was a photograph of one country in one year, and every bar was a generation carrying its own history upward. The wide middle bars were his own grandparents. The narrow base was, roughly, him.

He texted Marta a photo of the pyramid with the top circled. Can I use your guess, he typed, or does that make me a plagiarist. She wrote back within a minute: you can use it if you admit you didn't see it yourself. He laughed out loud, which made Pim look up from the chipmunk hole. That seemed fair, and also more than fair, because the honest version was better: a friend had looked at the shape and seen the reason before he had, and he could build on it without pretending otherwise. He would write that the top of the pyramid held more women than men because women lived longer than men on average, and that this shaped the demand for care as surely as the narrow base shaped the demand for schools.

What stayed uncertain, he decided, walking the last mile down with the light going amber through the pines, was everything the pyramid couldn't say: whether families would change, whether migration would widen the base, whether thirty years from now anyone would look at his prediction and call it obvious or call it naive. He would have to write that part too, the not knowing, and let it stand next to the parts he was sure of. At the trailhead he refolded the pyramid along its worn creases and held it out to Pim, who sniffed it once, thoroughly, and sneezed.

"All right," Olivier said, pocketing it again. "Home, then. We've got a future to get wrong."

activity: getting a first part-time job
story:
The kitchen at Marchetti's extruded steam from the pasta window in a steady ribbon, and Dylan stood beneath it in a borrowed apron that smelled of garlic and someone else's shift. He was seventeen, hired an hour ago at eleven dollars an hour, and already he had knocked over a bin of grated parmesan, swept it up, and been congratulated by the owner's daughter, Priya, for sweeping with commitment.

"Wash your hands like you mean it," she said. "Dad watches hands."

Mr. Marchetti watched everything from the pass, a squat man who moved slowly, as if conserving himself against the obsolescent equipment around him, the dented steamer, the slicer older than Dylan's parents. He had hired him on the strength of one question, asked over a Form I-9: "You here for the summer or for real?" Dylan had said for real, and it had felt true and also like a thing you say.

His first paycheck came two Fridays later, in a thin envelope Priya tossed him with a flick of her wrist like a card trick. Dylan read it leaning against the wait station, and his face fell before he could rearrange it. He counted hours on his fingers, quietly, then not quietly.

"Okay," he said. "I worked thirty-two hours. Thirty-two times eleven. That's three fifty-two. This says three thirty." He held the stub out as though it had personally wronged him. "Where'd twenty-two bucks go?"

"Tax," Priya said, stacking plates.

"What tax? I'm seventeen. Seventeen-year-olds are tax-exempt. That's a known fact."

"That is not a known fact." She took the stub from him and tapped a line. "See that? Social Security. Your employer withholds six point two percent of your wages for it."

Dylan stared at the line. "Six point two percent of everything?"

She shrugged. "Up to a yearly wage limit. Past that, it stops. Not a problem you'll have this year, dishwasher."

"So the government takes a cut of my dishwater." He did the math on a paper takeout menu, tongue between his teeth. "Six point two percent of three fifty-two, that's about twenty-one eighty. Plus whatever this other little guy is. Okay. Fine. It's not theft, it's arithmetic."

"Congratulations," Priya said. "You're an adult now. Your first adult feeling is disappointment at your paycheck."

That night he wrote to his older cousin Nadia, who was twenty-four and worked at a credit union in the city and answered family messages like a person doing a favor at gunpoint. He texted her a photo of the stub and a single question mark, then, because she demanded more, an actual message:

Dear Nadia, since you are the family's only financially literate member: Priya at work says my employer withholds 6.2 percent of my wages for Social Security, up to a yearly wage limit, and past that limit it stops. Is that real, or is she messing with me? Also is that money gone forever, or does it come back someday like some kind of annuity, paid out when I'm old? Please advise. Also hi. Your cousin, Dylan.

She replied at eleven, in her usual style, which was terse to the point of rudeness: "It's real. And yes, think of it as paying into something that pays back later, though don't build your retirement plan around a dishwashing job. Go to bed."

At work the next Saturday he found Priya restocking the soda cooler and told her, with the air of a man delivering a verdict, "I've confirmed your numbers with a professional."

"Your professional. The credit union one."

"She says hi."

"She's never met me."

"She says hi through me. It's a thing we do." He crouched to help her stack the two-liters. "Here's what I decided, though. I was mad, because it's my money and I earned it pushing plates around. But the money goes to people who already did their forty years of pushing plates around, and someday somebody's pushing plates around for me. That's if it all holds together. Nadia says don't build a retirement plan on it, and she's probably right, and I don't actually know what it'll look like in fifty years. So I've landed on: annoyed, but paying in anyway. Both at once."

"That's very mature of you," Priya said. "For a guy who told me Tuesday that seventeen-year-olds were tax-exempt."

"I said it with confidence. Confidence is different from being right. My dad taught me that."

Mr. Marchetti came around the corner with a tray of veal and paused long enough to look at the two of them crouched among the soda bottles. "In my country," he said, "you would not be texting and working at the same time."

"I'm working," Dylan said, holding up a two-liter in each hand as evidence.

"You're chatting," Mr. Marchetti said, but he was almost smiling. He set down the tray and pointed at the pasta window, where the steam extruded itself in its usual ribbon. "Water's boiling. Wednesday you learn the sauté station. Friday I'll teach you to slice prosciutto, and you will not cut yourself, because the slicer is older than my marriage and slower than my wife, God rest her patience."

Priya stood, dusting her knees. "He likes you," she said quietly. "He offered you the slicer. Marco worked here a year before the slicer."

Dylan carried the two two-liters to the wait station, set them down, and looked back at the old machine gleaming dully in the corner. Then he tied his apron tighter and went to find the boiling water.

story:
The flyer had promised snacks, which turned out to be a single tin of shortbread passed around a folding table in the common room of Maple Grove Seniors' Residence, where the basement food bank did its sorting on Saturdays. Vincent had signed up because his college application had demanded forty volunteer hours, his mother had demanded the application, and the hours had, mysteriously, never been logged. Now, with September looming and a form still blank, he sat between a woman named Dot who smelled of peppermint and a boy from his old school called Percy, who everyone agreed was insufferable but who could carry two boxes at once.

The work itself was simple enough that Vincent distrusted it. Cans and boxes came up from the donation bin in the loading dock, and the sorters checked labels, wiped dust, and stacked what was good on metal shelves while Percy narrated everything in a golf-announcer whisper. "Peaches, dented, risky. Rice, intact, a triumph. Beans, beans, the eternal beans." Vincent found the rhythm of it soothing, the small arithmetic of use versus waste, and he was stacking a row of tomato paste when he picked up a can of chickpeas, read the label, and dropped it straight into the discard bin with a flourish he privately found a little gratuitous.

Dot retrieved it before it hit the bottom. She held it up to the fluorescents, one eyebrow climbing toward her perm. "And what, may I ask, has this poor can done to you?"

"It's expired," Vincent said. "Well, past its date. Tenth of the month, and it's the sixteenth."

"Past its best before date," Dot said, and she said it the way his mother said "allegedly," with a whole courtroom behind it.

"Which means expired."

"Which means nothing of the sort. A best before date marks when the quality may start to decline, not when it becomes unsafe. Sealed food past that date may still be safe." She set the can back on the shelf with the tenderness of someone returning a rescued kitten. "Six days, dear. The chickpeas have more life in them than I do."

Percy leaned across Vincent, delighted. "So all this time you've been executing perfectly good chickpeas?"

"I've been executing chickpeas that said so themselves, on the label, in writing." Vincent picked up another can, turned it over, and hesitated with his hand over the discard bin like a man pausing at a gallows. The trouble was that he had grown up in a house where the date on the milk was law, where his father poured out yogurt on the stroke of midnight like some dairy Cinderella, and Dot's claim, delivered with total confidence by a woman who had also just told him she was ninety-one and had outlived three optometrists, sat uneasily beside all that inherited certainty. He didn't want to believe things just because someone said them with authority. On the other hand, he had just believed the label with no authority at all except ink.

"You're doing philosophy," Percy observed, mouth full of shortbread. "There's a whole word for it. Epistemology. How you know what you know. My cousin took a course and now he can't order lunch."

"I'm not doing philosophy. I'm doing chickpeas." But it was true that he was standing there weighing sources: the printed date, which told him nothing he could verify, against Dot, whose information at least came with a mechanism he could test. So he tested it. He carried the can, plus two others past their dates, to the residence's front office, where a young woman named Camille was stapling a newsletter, and he asked to use the computer. Four minutes later he came back down the hallway at a pace that startled a man with a walker, holding his phone like a torch.

"She's right," he announced. "Whole thing. Quality, not safety. Sealed food past the date may still be safe to eat. There's a government page and everything."

"I could have told you that," Dot said.

"You did tell me that. I just didn't believe you, which I want to apologize for, because apparently I trust a can more than a person." He restacked the discarded chickpeas on the shelf, then retrieved the ones from the morning's earlier stack, feeling like a man releasing wrongly convicted prisoners. It didn't entirely assuage his unease; some part of him still wanted a bright line, a date after which the world was simple, and he suspected that part of him would keep whispering at the back of the fridge for years. He was going to college in three weeks to learn how to know things, and here he'd spent the morning finding out he'd been doing it wrong over legumes.

"What about the crackers?" Percy called from the next table, holding up a box. "Best before the second. Still good, or are we crackers-lawyers now?"

"Put them on the shelf," Vincent said, and then, because the morning had earned it, "and Percy, one more golf commentary and you're sorting the beans alone."

"The beans," Percy said solemnly, "are the eternal beans."
